This iPhone App Lets You Take Photos By Clapping

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (398 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new iPhone camera app, HyperCam Trigger, aims to make it easier for mobile photographers to nail the perfect action shot, group portrait, or lightning photo.
  • According to recent reports, hyperCam Trigger uses various listening and detection methods to fire the iPhone’s camera at the right moment.
  • Meanwhile, for group portraits, which typically rely on a self-timer, HyperCam can listen for someone in the frame to clap, triggering an immediate shot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new iPhone camera app, HyperCam Trigger, aims to make it easier for mobile photographers to nail the perfect action shot, group portrait, or lightning photo.

According to recent reports, hyperCam Trigger uses various listening and detection methods to fire the iPhone’s camera at the right moment. For example, when photographing sports, children, or pets, the app can trip the shutter as soon as motion appears in the frame.

Meanwhile, for group portraits, which typically rely on a self-timer, HyperCam can listen for someone in the frame to clap, triggering an immediate shot. Users can customize the sensitivity for the app and the delay between detection and shooting.

According to recent reports, the app’s original purpose, which remains a core focus, was to make it easier to photograph lightning. It can use sound for this as well, though thunder arrives well after the flash of lightning itself. The app can also trigger a shot when it detects a sudden surge of light hitting the camera.

HyperCam can also trigger the shutter under other conditions, including camera shake, such as when the iPhone moves or tilts, or complete stability, such as when it is mounted on a tripod. Additionally, it can capture timelapse photos when it detects changes in light or motion, or wait to fire until someone in the frame smiles.

In a recent development, lightning triggers are not a new concept in photography. Photographers with DSLRs and mirrorless cameras have been using them for years, and new ones hit the market every so often, like the Bolt Hunter earlier this year.

Lightning triggers rely on the same principle as HyperCam: it is simply impossible for a photographer to manually press the shutter fast enough to catch fleeting events like lightning. Photographers can certainly try and can improve their odds by firing off long, rapid bursts of frames. However, assistance is required for consistent success.

HyperCam Trigger is available now in the App Store for free.

According to recent reports, however, some features are locked behind a paywall, including subject filters, short event video recording with frame extraction, detection zones, longer pre-trigger buffers, longer bursts, RAW recording, HDR, and more. HyperCam Pro is available for $3.99 per month, $22.99 per year, or $44.99 for lifetime access.

Apple’s Camera and Photo Software Lead Jon McCormack Has Retired

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (488 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jon McCormack, Apple’s head of photography and camera software development, has retired.
  • In a recent development, bloomberg reports that McCormack retired at the end of October.
  • Enhancement 11/20 @ 8 AM: McCormack shared this story on his Instagram, perhaps subtly confirming its accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jon McCormack, Apple’s head of photography and camera software development, has retired. A spectacular photographer in his own right, McCormack is stepping away, and his departure signals a major change for Apple regardless of the circumstances.

In a recent development, bloomberg reports that McCormack retired at the end of October. This information has not been independently verified, as at the time of publication, neither Apple nor McCormack has confirmed his departure.

Enhancement 11/20 @ 8 AM: McCormack shared this story on his Instagram, perhaps subtly confirming its accuracy.

According to recent reports, mcCormack, who was Apple’s vice president of camera and photo engineering, has been a major figure at the Silicon Valley giant since he arrived there in 2018. He oversaw the development of not only the iPhone camera system but also the camera software and all of the computational features that go along with it.

He was present for every briefing and discussion about the iPhone camera system through that time and became personally known to everyone at PetaPixel. He is also regularly quoted speaking about Apple’s philosophy regarding cameras and photography.

“Here’s our view of what a photograph is: The way we like to think of it is that it’s a personal celebration of something that really, actually happened,” he told PetaPixel back in 2024, just as generative AI was beginning its steady march into the creative industry. Apple has, since then, largely stayed that course.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps most importantly, McCormack is actually a photographer. In April, PetaPixel featured his most recent book, titled “Patterns: Art of the Natural World.”.

“I grew up on a farm in the Outback, Queensland in Australia,” McCormack mentioned. “Sheep and cattle property. We had no full-time electricity. We had a 32-volt generator that dad would run at night so that a little 12-inch black and white TV could be a thing. This is also when I got my first camera, my hand-me-down camera, and it wasn’t even my dad’s hand-me-down camera. It was my grandfather’s, a Minolta 35mm Mark IV made in either 1949 or 1950. I still have it.”.

His series made it abundantly clear that McCormack cares deeply about nature.

“My goal here is for people to look at our planet like a Fabergé egg,” McCormack explained. “It is unique, one of them in existence. It’s fragile, it’s intricate, it’s beautiful. It’s something to be protected and taken care of, and it’s something you can fall in love with.”.

It’s hard to think of a greater loss for Apple than McCormack. It is unlikely that Apple will find someone who is nearly as talented or who cares as much about photography as a fine art. PetaPixel is hard-pressed to believe there was anyone better for his role at the company than he was.

Miami artists’ Art Basel boycott campaign calls for alternatives to fair week’s commercial model

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1141 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, as Art Basel Miami Beach prepares to return to the city, a group of local artists and organisers is asking the Miami art community to reconsider its relationship with the busy week of fairs that takes over the city every December.
  • Industry observers note that in a city whose international cultural profile has become virtually inseparable from the Art Basel brand, the boycott poses a difficult question: can Miami’s arts economy sustain its local creative community without depending so heavily on the machinery of a global art fair?
  • “We realise that in order to refuse to take part in something as intertwined and culturally impactful as Art Basel, you really have to start building an alternative,” says misael soto, an artist and founder of Artists 4 Artists Miami.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, as Art Basel Miami Beach prepares to return to the city, a group of local artists and organisers is asking the Miami art community to reconsider its relationship with the busy week of fairs that takes over the city every December. The grassroots collective Artists 4 Artists Miami announced aims for its “Art Basel Boycott” at a protest outside the Miami Beach Convention Center at the end of last year’s edition of the Switzerland-based fair. Now, after a year of preparation, the collective is launching its first campaign, inviting local artists, curators, gallerists, collectors and residents to reconsider their participation in Miami Art Week’s fairs while building alternatives rooted in the community.

Industry observers note that in a city whose international cultural profile has become virtually inseparable from the Art Basel brand, the boycott poses a difficult question: can Miami’s arts economy sustain its local creative community without depending so heavily on the machinery of a global art fair? Organisers are not calling for a blanket rejection of Miami Art Week or even its tentpole event. Instead, organisers envision a longer-term effort to challenge the economic and political structures surrounding the fair and redirect attention toward local artists, independent galleries and experimental programming.

“We realise that in order to refuse to take part in something as intertwined and culturally impactful as Art Basel, you really have to start building an alternative,” says misael soto, an artist and founder of Artists 4 Artists Miami.

In a recent development, the campaign grew out of the collective’s broader efforts to connect cultural work with other grassroots struggles. After spending much of 2025 supporting campaigns led by other organisations, Artists 4 Artists Miami began considering how it could mobilise its own community. Its participation in protests organised by Jewish Voice for Peace and other groups opposing the war in Gaza helped crystallise the idea, soto says, prompting organisers to examine the connections between the art market, housing affordability, labour conditions, and the companies that benefit from the fair.

Recent findings suggest that for soto, Art Basel has become a focal point for these overlapping concerns. The fair generates significant economic activity, but the group questions how much of that value reaches Miami’s working artists and residents, particularly as the city becomes increasingly expensive. The group also points to the environmental and infrastructural costs of hosting an international event, and to the political and corporate interests associated with some of its major partners and investors.

Those concerns extend to the fair’s relationship with the city itself; soto points to a recent Miami Beach Commission decision concerning Art Basel’s rental agreement for the Miami Beach Convention Center, which reduced the fair’s rent from nearly $1m to around $500,000 and committed the equivalent of an additional $300,000 in public funds toward first-responder and security costs. The group questions whether the benefits the fair brings to the community justify the public resources devoted to it.

Industry observers note that and yet, as the Artists 4 Artists Miami organisers acknowledge, Art Basel is deeply embedded in Miami’s cultural identity and economy. For many artists and arts workers, Miami Art Week provides essential income through art handling, installation, production and other contract jobs, while offering a smaller number opportunities to exhibit their work. Local galleries rely on the annual influx of collectors, press and visitors, and cultural institutions benefit from the attention and potential donor relationships the week brings.

Recent findings suggest that “Art Basel Miami Beach has been a committed partner to Miami Beach and its creative community for more than two decades, supporting local artists and organisations through cultural programming, educational initiatives and opportunities for artistic exchange,” a spokesperson for Art Basel tells The Art Newspaper. “The fair also generates significant economic activity across the region, benefiting local businesses and workers in a wide range of sectors.”.

Sources indicate that according to local officials, the 2025 edition of Art Basel Miami Beach generated nearly $60m in economic impact for the city of Miami Beach, and $570m in economic impact for Miami-Dade County. The fair has consistently included several South Florida galleries as exhibitors, and every year the city of Miami Beach acquires a work from the fair for its public art collection.

Recent findings suggest that ariel Lynch, an artist and educator who has lived in the city for four years, signed the Artists 4 Artists Miami pledge despite recognising the tensions inherent in the campaign. Lynch notes the fair offers substantial economic benefits to established galleries and collectors while providing comparatively few exhibition opportunities for local artists.

“Miami deserves more than institutions like Art Basel Miami Beach,” Lynch claims. She looks to spend Miami Art Week visiting local galleries, events and experimental exhibitions instead of attending the main fair, while introducing students to the city’s year-round art scene.

Still, Lynch acknowledges the difficult position facing those who depend on Art Basel for their livelihoods. For workers already struggling to make ends meet, declining paid work during Miami Art Week may not be financially feasible. That is a dilemma soto is also mindful of: the fairs have helped pay their bills and enabled them to travel internationally, but they believe the short-term benefits can obscure longer-term costs, including overwork, underappreciated labour and environmental strain.

The “Art Basel Boycott” pledge is designed to accommodate different levels of participation. Signatories must select at least one commitment: not attending Art Basel Miami Beach, not exhibiting work at the fair, not exhibiting during Miami Art Week or withholding their labour from the fair. They can also choose commitments aimed at supporting alternatives, allowing participants to assess what is realistic given their circumstances.

As of this writing, the campaign had collected 21 signatures through an online form hosted on the collective’s website. Organisers are contacting local cultural and political organisations, particularly grassroots groups, to seek endorsements and establish partnerships. One existing partner is Panamía, a local network connecting businesses, creatives and residents. Artists 4 Artists Miami is also exploring programming in conjunction with a Panamía gathering and art print fair planned for Miami Art Week.

Beyond events, the collective hopes to establish a mutual-support network that could help pledge signatories navigate the financial consequences of opting out of Miami Art Week. That would entail connecting artists and organisations with local resources, soto claims, including food assistance and other forms of mutual aid.

For the boycott’s organisers and signatories, success will not necessarily be measured by a signature count or an immediate impact on the fair. Instead, they hope the campaign will encourage a gradual shift in how Miami’s cultural producers and workers understand their economic and political influence.

“If a year from now we see that much more alternative and locally focused programming happening outside of Art Week,” soto says, “that would be a huge victory.”.

According to recent reports, with more creators capturing both photos and videos, accessory makers are stepping up to meet the demand. Heipi’s newly introduced 2-in-1 hybrid tripod head for photo and video promises the best of both worlds.

Photographers often like ball heads because they are versatile, easy to adjust, and stable. By loosening the head, photographers can promptly recompose their shots. However, ball heads are not as easy to control or as smooth for panning motion as a traditional pan-tilt fluid head, which videographers typically prefer. Further, Heipi notes its latest head also delivers the balancing performance of a gimbal head, a popular choice for wildlife and birding photographers with huge, heavy lenses.

Industry observers note that “Today, the line between photography and videography is becoming increasingly blurred. During a single shoot, creators may switch between wide-angle and telephoto lenses, move from still photography to video, and capture a wider range of perspectives and moments,” Heipi writes on Kickstarter. “Yet different shooting needs often call for different support equipment: a ball head, a gimbal head, a fluid head, and more. Carrying multiple heads adds bulk to your gear and extra weight to every journey.”.

Heipi believes its latest hybrid head offers all the benefits of separate tripod heads in a single package.

Recent findings suggest that the Heipi KB50 2-in-1 Hybrid Head weighs 560 grams (just over 1.2 pounds) and is about the size of a traditional ball head. However, it can instantly switch from ball head mode to pan-tilt mode, and videographers can screw on a grip for even more control.

It has been revealed that heipi’s latest tripod head also features a stepless counterbalance system designed for gear weighing from 1.5 to 5 kilograms (3.3 to 11 pounds). That encompasses a wide range of equipment, including those significant, heavy supertelephoto lenses mentioned earlier.

The KB50 features a standard 3/8″-16 UNC female thread on its base, allowing it to attach to a wide variety of tripod legs. It also includes an Arca-Swiss clamp.

In a recent development, the Heipi KB50 2-in-1 Hybrid Head is available to back on Kickstarter now, starting at $428, which is a $120 discount compared to the $548 MSRP. Heipi claims it will begin shipping in April 2027. With just over 40 days left in the campaign, Heipi has already shattered its $10,000 goal.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Ateliers Jean Nouvel.

French architecture studio Ateliers Jean Nouvel has shared photos revealing construction progress on the giant Shenzhen Opera House, due for completion in China in 2028.

Located on the Shekou Peninsula overlooking Shenzhen Bay, the opera house will eventually be defined by an elongated, wavy roofscape, nodding to the site’s connection to the sea.

Pritzker Prize-winning architect Jean Nouvel’s studio has designed it as a new cultural landmark for the city, with a 2,300-seat concert hall, an 1,800-seat theatre and an 800-seat venue among its facilities.

The construction photos help visualise the scale of the 250,000-square-metre opera house, with its various facilities sprawling out across its waterfront site.

They showcase its main concert hall with its horseshoe-shaped blueprint, alongside the two smaller performance venues.

Ateliers Jean Nouvel’s design for Shenzhen Opera House was the winning entry of an invited international architecture competition, for which other entrants included BIG, Snøhetta, MVRDV and Kengo Kuma.

Alongside the main performance halls, it will contain a multifunctional theatre with 400 seats, cultural spaces, backstage areas, apartments for performers and offices.

To help further connect the building to the surrounding water, the interior is expected to feature iridescent materials such as mother-of-pearl, also known as nacre.

“The sea will be both around you and over you,” explained Nouvel when the project was revealed in 2021.

“This explains more clearly why the main foyer has to be made of a noble, precious and luminous material that spells the meeting of sea and music and light,” Nouvel continued.

“Using the lustrous white reflections of a nacreous material will be a concrete poeticisation of the meeting of the sea and the auditorium and concert halls of the Opera House.”.

French architect Nouvel founded his eponymous studio in 1994. We recently reported on the news that the studio’s La Querola housing development in Andorra, designed with Spanish studio Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos, was damaged in a fire. The project won the housing category of this year’s Dezeen Awards, which took place last night.

Another landmark opera house recently featured on Dezeen is the Shanghai Grand Opera House, designed by Snøhetta with a giant spiral staircase.

Images courtesy of Ateliers Jean Nouvel.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Associated Press is moving eight photo editor positions to India today, in a move condemned by unions.
  • The roles are right now carried out in the United States, but today is their last day.
  • “AP is at it again,” the AP News Guild wrote on X last week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Associated Press is moving eight photo editor positions to India today, in a move condemned by unions.

The roles are right now carried out in the United States, but today is their last day. The offshoring follows similar moves this summer, when AP laid off 20 video production jobs in the U.S. and moved them to its hub in Noida, India.

“AP is at it again,” the AP News Guild wrote on X last week. “The News Media Guild learned Monday that AP will offshore eight photo positions after already gutting its U.S. video production team.”.

In a statement, the News Media Guild president Kimberlee Krusei called AP’s move “union busting.”.

“Fewer people, fewer communities being covered, and less news. That’s the impact of today’s decision,” says Krusei. “AP’s newsgathering has gone beyond ‘lean’ to leaving many coverage areas abandoned. The remaining journalists are asked to do the impossible and it shows.”.

The Guild indicates that far from just picking photos taken by AP photographers, the editors provide direction, guide the photographers, correct essential information, and scrutinize images for alterations.

In a recent development, “They bring decades of local knowledge, news judgment and connections. They negotiate with outside photographers to buy the rights to photos — a now essential part of covering breaking news.”.

One of the affected photo editors, Pablo Salinas, who is based in Newly introduced York, says that he went above and beyond in 2019 when he obtained the rights to a shocking photo of a drowned father and daughter lying face down in the Rio Grande River.

Recent findings suggest that “That was a picture that I don’t think any other photo editor would have been able to get,” states Salinas. “Because it wasn’t ours, I scoured social media and found it and got in touch with the photographer. And she reluctantly gave us permission to use it.”.

The photo went viral and became part of the story about the border crisis.

“AP benefits from having photo editors that are local to where the news is being produced,” says AP photographer Matt Rourke.

“It’s a partnership,” adds Salinas. “The kind of partnership you lose when you sacrifice these jobs to save a few dollars.”.

According to recent reports, photo editors are intimately involved in the biggest stories of the day. They might be working closely with local photographers to move hundreds of shots illustrating crucial election results. Or securing the rights to sensitive images that convey difficult news. AP’s Pablo Salinas went in front of the camera to talk about the partnership that’s lost when news leaders sacrifice jobs like his. Tell the company their valuable work can’t just be done from anywhere at this link: https://t.co/euBigYM1tt.

— AP News Guild (@APNewsGuild) November 12, 2026.

An AP spokesperson tells TheWrap that the agency is respecting and following the collective bargaining agreement.

“This is part of the changes we announced over the summer to significantly scale our visual production capabilities at our latest hub in Noida, India, where we have added dozens of talented journalists to our global news organization,” the spokesperson states.

The AP indicates that its hub in Noida will soon employ nearly 100 video producers and photo editors.

With its approximately 35mm equivalent focal length, Thypoch’s first autofocus lens for Fujifilm X mount and first autofocus prime lens period is well-suited to a wide range of photographic applications. The 35mm focal length is a classic one for a reason. It works well for street, landscapes, portraits, and travel, to name a few go-to genres.

In a recent development, thypoch has long been associated with classically-inspired manual focus lenses, like the Simera 50mm f/1.4 and Ksana 21mm f/3.5. Recent findings suggest that the latest Thypoch AF 23mm f/1.4 Sculptor is styled much like the Voyager, with diagonal lines and a vintage-inspired yet modern design. Although beauty is subjective, the Sculptor will likely earn a few fans thanks to its handsome looks.

It's ultimately what's on the inside that counts, though. Inside the Sculptor, 12 lens elements are arranged across ten groups, promising edge-to-edge sharpness even at the maximum f/1.4 aperture. A 10-bladed aperture diaphragm sits behind the glass.

Industry observers note that the lens is also quite compact, measuring just 71.4 millimeters (2.8 inches) long with a 52mm front filter thread. The lens weighs 283 grams (just under 10 ounces).

Recent findings suggest that the autofocus prime can focus as close as 0.25 meters (0.82 feet), giving a maximum magnification of about 0.13x. It's definitely not a macro lens.

According to recent reports, the Sculptor's most obvious competitor is Fujifilm's own XF 23mm f/1.4 R LM WR lens, which costs $1,049.95. Fujifilm's lens weighs 375 grams (13.2 ounces) and is 77.8 millimeters (3.1 inches) long. Thypoch's new lens is much lighter and more affordable.

SSdH "renegotiates light" in Melbourne warehouse transformation

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A double-height glass atrium draws light into the open-strategy interior of Tucker, a former warehouse that Australian architecture practice SSdH has turned into a residence and exhibition space in Melbourne.
  • For the project, SSdH wanted to focus on adaptation over replacement and aimed to work as much as possible with the existing warehouse structure.
  • The studio designed a raised courtyard, a steel-mesh external stair tower and a double-height atrium to draw more natural light into the 770-square-metre space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Pier Carthew.

A double-height glass atrium draws light into the open-strategy interior of Tucker, a former warehouse that Australian architecture practice SSdH has turned into a residence and exhibition space in Melbourne.

For the project, SSdH wanted to focus on adaptation over replacement and aimed to work as much as possible with the existing warehouse structure.

The studio designed a raised courtyard, a steel-mesh external stair tower and a double-height atrium to draw more natural light into the 770-square-metre space.

To help retain the character of the former warehouse, SSdH fitted the main entrance into its loading bay and preserved a ghost sign overhead.

The Galvabond-clad entry was designed to act as a “deliberately compressed” holding zone, SSdH noted, suspending visitors within a relatively unlit area before opening onto the light-drenched central space.

“Light was a big part of the original brief, with the existing boundary walls, limited openings and previous additions leaving much of the warehouse interior quite dark”, SSdH told Dezeen.

“We liked the idea of being held for a moment, making the shift in scale and light feel more surprising”.

In a recent development, next to the main entrance, SSdH placed a double-storey external stairway that leads to a roof terrace. This was clad in steel mesh to allow for natural light and views from the first-floor interiors.

The ground floor interior is dominated by a double-height glass and steel atrium that was angled against the original floor strategy of the warehouse to let light into the open-plan living area.

“Our approach begins with looking at what’s already there rather than trying to make something entirely fresh”, SSdH remarked.

“We were interested in how the building could continue to evolve through smaller adjustments rather than extensive demolition”.

The studio designed the interior of the home to be “continuously adaptable”, with the ground floor able to be used as an exhibition space.

Much of the floor plan is given over to open space, with a curation of select furnishings anchoring it.

In the living area, built-in sofas line the perimeter of the atrium wall next to the courtyard, and are accompanied by an industrial-informed timber and shearling bench by design studio BMDO.

In the kitchen, SSdH added a monolithic travertine island that is complemented by spotted-gum-timber and stainless-steel cabinetry that was fitted against a preserved painted-brick wall.

“Throughout, the material palette is honest, refined and robust, allowing the characters of the original warehouse to remain present”, remarked SSdH.

A wooden staircase set within a double-height void leads to the first floor, which features wraparound circulation and is home to the private bedrooms and bathrooms.

Spotted-gum and major-river timber cladding was used across cabinetry, extended doorways and flooring, with exposed roof trusses visible throughout. Both bedrooms receive ample light from south and north-facing windows, with the primary bedroom overlooking the atrium and courtyard below.

The main bathroom is fitted with wraparound marble and features a glass brick exterior wall that SSdH added as part of its aim to “renegotiate light” within the existing framework of the warehouse.

“We were drawn to the thickness and form of the glass, which catches, holds and releases light in a way that conventional textured glazing doesn’t quite achieve,” the studio said.

Overall, SSdH hoped to preserve the charm of the original warehouse while creating an adaptable, contemporary space.

Many decisions were “made on site as the building revealed itself”, the studio stated.

“We wanted the spaces to remain open to different ways and possibilities of living, allowing the building to adapt without needing to be completely reworked in the future”, it concluded.

Other Melbourne homes recently featured on Dezeen include a studio with a “lantern-like” glass-block facade, a century-old corner shop transformed into a family home and a home comprised of a cluster of red-brick volumes.

Photography by Pier Carthew.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A drone operator filmed English soccer team Manchester United’s first training session with newly introduced coach Mauricio Pochettino and shared the “unethical” footage on YouTube.

According to recent reports, pochettino officially left the U.S. men’s national soccer team (USMNT) to become head coach of English Premier League club Manchester United. On Thursday, he oversaw his first training session with Man United’s first-team squad ahead of Sunday’s Premier League game against Liverpool at the club’s Carrington training ground.

However, a drone operator who runs the YouTube account CC Overview — which describes itself as sharing “drone footage of construction at football stadia and events affecting our environment” — flew his aerial device over the facility during Pochettino’s first training session. He then posted a 12-minute segment on YouTube on Thursday.

According to a report by The Athletic, Pochettino and his players, who were split into three groups, were identifiable in the aerial footage, which amassed over 600,000 views on YouTube. The footage indicated Pochettino leading a training session with one group of players, while his assistant Jesus Perez oversaw two separate groups. The video, filmed at United’s Carrington training base, also captured audio of the YouTuber apparently controlling the drone saying “let’s get closer,” before zooming in on the newly introduced head coach.

The drone operator has since apologized for a “total error in judgment.” He states the aerial footage was legal under U.K. drone laws but has removed the “unethical” video from YouTube.

“A total error of judgement on my part led to me filming some of the Man United training session at Carrington, whilst the flight was legal in terms of drone laws I fully accept it was unethical on my part,” the drone operator writes in a post on YouTube.

The drone operator describes aiming to film Pochettino in the club’s training kit for the first time, but adds he had no intention of recording a “meaningful training session.” The YouTuber states he was operating under an incorrect assumption that it was open to media outlets. He also insists he acted independently and was not working on behalf of Liverpool or any other football club.

“I would like to apologize to Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino and the players for my actions and sincerely hope those actions do not affect the outcome of any match,” the drone operator notes.

Man United prohibits the use of drones at its Carrington training facility, where signs warn that anyone operating a drone could face civil action or prosecution.

In the U.K., capturing aerial footage using drones is permitted provided operators comply with Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) safety regulations, as well as privacy and data protection laws.

CAA guidance on privacy for drone use details: “If you use these devices where people can expect privacy, such as inside their home or garden, you’re likely to be breaking data protection laws.” It adds that drone operators should “let people know before you start recording or taking pictures”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Syrian photographer has finally been reunited with his personal photo archive more than a decade after hiding it behind a wall he built during the country’s war.

Photographer Ahmed al-Bekkar fled Syria more than a decade ago, seeking refuge in Turkey amid widespread destruction, looting, and attacks by the terrorist group ISIS (Daesh) and forces loyal to Syria’s now-topled Assad regime, according to a report by Anadolu Agency.

‘Every piece of paper has a history, every page holds a memory’.

🇸🇾 Syrian photographer Ahmed al-Bekkar recovers personal archive in Raqqa after more than a decade.

● Bekkar, 66, sealed his library before fleeing war to protect books, photographs and personal documents.

● He sought refuge in Türkiye amid attacks by Daesh (ISIS) and forces of ousted Syrian regime.

— Anadolu English (@anadoluagency) November 19, 2026.

Industry observers note that before leaving Syria, Bekkar built a wall to conceal the entrance to his personal library in the northern city of Raqqa, hoping to protect his extensive photographic archive. The archive contains approximately 3,000 printed photographs of Raqqa, as well as a much larger digital collection documenting historical sites, cities, and markets across Syria.

Sources indicate that during his decade in Turkey, the now 66-year-old photographer continued his photographic work, helping establish the House of Migrants association and the Turkish-Arab Art House. Although Bekkar spent productive years doing photography in the Turkish capital of Istanbul, he says nothing could replace his hometown in Syria.

Anadolu Agency reports that Bekkar returned to Raqqa this year and reopened the library he had concealed behind the wall more than a decade earlier. The photographer describes watching the bricks being removed one by one from the wall as an emotional experience, having long dreamed of setting foot inside his archive again.

Sources indicate that “Every piece of paper has a history, every page holds a memory. I spent time and effort obtaining and preserving every document,” the photographer tells the news outlet. “I feel that those days are preserved in these papers, whose owners are no longer with us, but which have remained behind.”.

Bekkar recalled growing up across from an old mosque in Raqqa, where the surrounding historical buildings inspired his interest in photography and Syria’s cultural heritage. Since returning to his hometown, Bekkar has revisited historical sites he photographed years earlier to document them now.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of Vincent van Gogh’s last paintings, long hidden from public view, sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees) at Sotheby’s New York on Wednesday (18 November), breaking the artist’s auction record.
  • According to recent reports, but the landmark results were high points for an evening of uneven bidding, with just more than one-third of works selling for below their pre-sale estimates.
  • Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), the most valuable lot offered across Fresh York’s auction houses this season, had attracted attention even before reaching the rostrum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of Vincent van Gogh’s last paintings, long hidden from public view, sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees) at Sotheby’s New York on Wednesday (18 November), breaking the artist’s auction record. The result helped propel two back-to-back sales to a combined $663.26m ($777.8m with fees), with additional auction records for Mary Cassatt and Aaron Douglas.

According to recent reports, but the landmark results were high points for an evening of uneven bidding, with just more than one-third of works selling for below their pre-sale estimates. The Blaquier-Arrieta collection, billed as the most valuable collection to come to auction in New York this season, brought in $358m ($412m with fees), falling short of its roughly $450m estimate. Sotheby’s Modern Evening sale, which followed immediately afterwards, generated another $305.21m ($365.8m with fees) against a $260.2m to $378.4m overall estimate.

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), the most valuable lot offered across Fresh York’s auction houses this season, had attracted attention even before reaching the rostrum. One of Van Gogh’s final paintings before his death in 1890, the work had for decades been out of public view in the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, built by Argentine sugar industry heiress Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and her husband, Carlos Pedro Blaquier, who served as president of Argentina’s largest sugar producer. Just a day before the sale, Sotheby’s unveiled that a settlement had been reached between the Blaquier heirs and the heirs of the painting’s previous owners, Hedwig and Samuel Fischer, following questions about the work’s Nazi-era provenance.

According to recent reports, van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890) sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees). Courtesy Sotheby's.

In a recent development, estimated to fetch around $180m, the painting hammered at $165m ($190.4m with fees) after nearly five minutes of bidding, eventually going to a bidder in the room—William Acquavella, the head of Acquavella Galleries. Despite the hammer price falling short of its estimate, the Sotheby’s-guaranteed work surpassed Van Gogh’s previous auction record of $117m with fees, set in 2022 when Orchard with Cypresses (1888) sold at Christie’s Paul Allen sale. The result also made it the second most valuable object ever sold at Sotheby’s, behind Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16), which fetched $236.4m with fees during last November’s marquee sales, and the fourth most valuable painting ever sold at auction.

Soon afterwards, Paul Cézanne’s Arlequin (1888-90) came to the rostrum. The painting, the last of the artist’s four works from the series still in public hands, hammered at $99m ($111m with fees), falling short of its $120m estimate. It also failed to surpass Cézanne’s auction record, set during the same 2022 Paul Allen sale at Christie’s New York, when the landscape La Montagne Sainte-Victoire (1888-90) fetched $138m with fees. Nevertheless, Arlequin became the most valuable Cézanne painting from the Harlequin series to sell at auction.

Ultimately, six of the collection’s 12 lots hammered below their low estimates, while five sold within or at their estimate ranges. Just one work exceeded expectations: the final lot, Camille Pissarro’s Maison de Piette à Montfoucault, effet de neige, avec un homme portant un fagot (1875), which hammered at $1.62m ($2m with fees), against a $700,000 to $900,000 estimate.

The subsequent Modern Evening sale generated $305.21m ($365.8m with fees), although bidding was similarly patchy. Of the works sold, 14 hammered below their low estimates, 21 sold within their estimate ranges and 11 exceeded their high estimates.

According to recent reports, the top lot was René Magritte’s L’Ami de l’ordre (1964), which hammered at $39m ($45.5m with fees), far surpassing its $25m to $35m estimate. Combining the artist’s signature bowler-hatted figure with a nighttime landscape, the painting was consigned by the estate of beauty pioneer Sydell Miller. Two years ago, 25 works from her collection brought in $215.9m with fees during a single-owner auction at Sotheby’s November marquee sales. According to Sotheby’s, only one related composition now remains in private hands. L’Ami de l’ordre is the most valuable Magritte painting featuring a bowler hat to sell at auction.

Harriet Tubman (1931) by Aaron Douglas. Courtesy Sotheby's.

It has been revealed that one of the evening’s most exciting results came courtesy of the Harlem Renaissance artist Aaron Douglas, whose Harriet Tubman (1931) shattered his previous auction record. The painting depicts the American abolitionist with her arms raised overhead, breaking a chain amid a leafy landscape and a smoking cannon. Estimated at $2.5m to $3.5m, it hammered at $12m ($14.48m with fees) after a seven-minute bidding battle. At one point, the competition pitted father and daughter against each other on the telephones, bidding on behalf of their respective clients: George Wachter, Sotheby’s chairman of the Americas, and Jacqueline Wachter, vice-chairman of private sales for contemporary art and head of the Los Angeles office. The result far surpassed Douglas’s previous auction record of $600,000, set at Swann in 2008. Proceeds from the sale will benefit Bennett College, one of just two historically Black women’s colleges in the US.

According to recent reports, mary Cassatt also established a upcoming auction record when Summertime (1894–95) hammered at $11m ($13.3m with fees) to an online bidder, exceeding its $7m to $10m estimate. The result surpassed her previous record of $7.49m, set at Christie’s New York in 2022. The painting came from the collection of the late oil tycoon Armand Hammer, with proceeds benefiting his eponymous foundation.

It has been revealed that only one lot failed to sell: Remedios Varo’s El vagabundo, which passed at $1.5m. Three other works, by Henri Matisse, Cézanne and Magritte, were withdrawn during the sale. Together, the withdrawn lots carried estimates totalling between $12.5m and $18.5m.

Adobe Ends Free Creative Cloud Subscriptions for Stock Photographers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Adobe will no longer offer complimentary Creative Cloud subscriptions to photographers who sell their work through Adobe Stock, replacing the scheme with discounts instead.
  • For years, Adobe has incentivized photographers to contribute to its picture marketplace by dangling the carrot of a free subscription to Photoshop and other Adobe apps.
  • Robert Kneschke, a professional stock photographer based in Germany who runs the Daily Life of a Photo Producer blog, indicates that in 2020, a photographer needed 150 sales to unlock a free Adobe Photography initiative, while 5,000 downloads would net them complete access to Creative Cloud.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Adobe will no longer offer complimentary Creative Cloud subscriptions to photographers who sell their work through Adobe Stock, replacing the scheme with discounts instead.

For years, Adobe has incentivized photographers to contribute to its picture marketplace by dangling the carrot of a free subscription to Photoshop and other Adobe apps.

Robert Kneschke, a professional stock photographer based in Germany who runs the Daily Life of a Photo Producer blog, indicates that in 2020, a photographer needed 150 sales to unlock a free Adobe Photography initiative, while 5,000 downloads would net them complete access to Creative Cloud.

According to recent reports, but Adobe has recently made changes to its bonus program, changing the eligibility and prizes. Instead of offering full complimentary access, Adobe is offering a 70% discount on Creative Cloud Pro to the first 500 contributors who generate 6,500 downloads and submit over 1,000 newly introduced images.

The 70% discount is also on offer to the first 500 contributors who “have 10 or more datasets and maintain high quality standards.” It’s not entirely clear what a dataset is from a photographer’s perspective. On its website, Adobe describes it as a “storage and management construct for a collection of data, typically a table, that contains a schema (columns) and fields (rows).”.

There’s also a 40% discount on offer for Creative Cloud Pro for the first 10,000 contributors who generate more than 2,500 sales as well as submitting over “100 pieces of unique content.”.

Sources indicate that the above criteria must be met from September 22, 2026, to March 12, 2027. The codes will be handed out in April.

Adobe will still provide full complimentary access to Creative Cloud Pro to photographers who are “actively commissioned to create content and/or require Adobe tools to fulfill project requirements.”.

Writing on his blog, Kneschke calls the changes a “clear step backward” while speculating that the datasets are for AI training purposes.

“A gift has become a discount voucher,” Kneschke notes. “Along with the lower royalties, this is further evidence that Adobe is cutting costs at the expense of photographers.”.

Earlier this year, PetaPixel reported on Gerald Carter, the owner of Diversity Photos, and his fight with Adobe after he discovered that the company trained its AI image generator Firefly on his entire photo library.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Warning: The following photos contains content that some may find upsetting.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that three photographers have sued the St. Paul Police Department in Minnesota over its alleged use of chemical munitions against them during an ICE raid, with their own photographs documenting the incident.

Warning: The following photos contains content that some may find upsetting.

In a recent development, aaron Nesheim, a photographer for Sahan Journal, MPR News photojournalist Kerem Yücel, and freelance photographer Timothy Evans filed the lawsuit against the St. Paul Police Department on Tuesday. The photographers accuse officers of firing pepper balls at them, pepper-spraying them at close range, and deploying tear gas against them while they were covering a demonstration.

Recent findings suggest that the lawsuit stems from an incident on November 25 last year, when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents attempted to arrest a man at his home in the Payne-Phalen neighborhood of St. Paul, Minnesota. A growing crowd of protesters gathered outside the property as federal agents attempted to detain the man.

Sources indicate that nesheim, Yücel, and Evans arrived at the scene to document the protest. All three photographers carried large professional cameras and wore press passes around their necks. Evans also wore a ballistic vest labeled “PRESS.”.

In a recent development, according to a report by the Minnesota Reformer, St. Paul police officers also responded to the scene. After ICE agents left with the detainees, protesters demanded that local police leave as well. As the officers withdrew, they fired pepper balls and used pepper spray and tear gas against both protesters and photojournalists.

According to court documents, an officer pepper-sprayed Yücel at close range while he was photographing the scene. The lawsuit says that the photographer inhaled and swallowed the chemicals. Other officers fired pepper balls at Yücel, striking him in the neck, shoulders, and chest.

In a recent development, according to the complaint, the three photographers were standing together off to the side of the crowd, at least 10 feet from the nearest protesters and out of the way of law enforcement officers. Despite this, police allegedly fired pepper balls and debuted tear gas at the photographers.

All three photographers experienced irritation to their eyes and airways following exposure to the chemicals. Yücel struggled to breathe and was taken from the scene by ambulance. According to MPR News, Yücel was forced to put his jacket into a garbage bag to prevent the chemicals from affecting the crew and staff at Regions Hospital mentioned they could not admit Yücel into the main hospital because the chemical irritants on his body and clothing posed a safety risk to staff and other patients.

According to recent reports, evans suffered severe abdominal bruising after a pepper ball exploded inside his ballistic vest, while Nesheim was struck in the head by a police projectile. All three photojournalists required mental health treatment following the incident.

In a recent development, the photographers argue in their lawsuit that the St. Paul Police Department’s actions violated their rights under the First, Fourth, and Fourteenth Amendments of the U.S. Constitution and constituted assault and battery, among other violations. They are seeking damages, attorney’s fees, and a court order barring the St. Paul Police Department from engaging in further unconstitutional conduct against them.

“The use of this tear gas, like the use of the pepper balls, was clearly meant as retaliation for plaintiffs’ exercise of their First Amendment rights,”attorney Kevin Riach writes. “The officers could not have been shooting at anyone other than Nesheim, Yücel and Evans, who were all clustered within several feet of one another.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Association of Photographers (AOP) has declared the 36 finalists for its 2026 AOP Open Awards, a competition celebrating still and moving images by professional and amateur photographers from around the world.
  • Now in its 20th year, the competition allows photographers of all experience levels to compete on equal terms.
  • The finalists’ work will be exhibited at Fujifilm House of Photography in London from January 29 to March 14, 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Association of Photographers (AOP) has declared the 36 finalists for its 2026 AOP Open Awards, a competition celebrating still and moving images by professional and amateur photographers from around the world.

Now in its 20th year, the competition allows photographers of all experience levels to compete on equal terms. Sponsored by Capture One, Fujifilm UK, and Maxima, this year’s awards are divided into three formats: single image, series, and moving image.

The finalists’ work will be exhibited at Fujifilm House of Photography in London from January 29 to March 14, 2027. The Gold and Silver winners will be unveiled at a private viewing on the evening of January 28.

It has been revealed that the Best in Show winner will receive £1,250 ($1,600), while the Gold and Silver winners will take home £250 and £100, respectively. Additional prizes from the sponsors and AOP membership are also on offer.

The 36 shortlisted works cover a wide range of subjects, from LGBTIQ+ communities in the remote jungles of Suriname to Muslim women competing in Tbourida, an equestrian sport with roots in 16th-century battle tactics.

Recent findings suggest that other projects explore the tradition of workers, local clubs, and Sunday league teams playing football on London’s Hackney Marshes, alongside images of the game being played away from conventional pitches in Morocco. Elsewhere, photographers document the 40,000 Elvis impersonators and fans who descend on Porthcawl, a small seaside town in South Wales, for the world’s largest Elvis Presley festival.

The finalists also include a portrait of a woman continuing to run her family’s flower business in Kyiv throughout the war in Ukraine, portraits of national treasures David Hockney and Dame Judi Dench, and a visual ode to gratitude for skin.

All 36 finalist projects can be viewed on the AOP Awards website.

The AOP Open Awards accept entries without categories or prescribed themes, leaving photographers free to submit work that is either personal or commissioned. The competition welcomes still photography, moving images, and creative uses of technology and innovation in work produced by a person. AI-generated images are not accepted, and all entries must have been created on or after January 1, 2025.

DxO Year in Review 2026: Four Latest Versions and Where Each One Fits in Your Edit

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2873 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A lot changed in DxO’s photo editing tools in 2026.
  • Together, DxO’s software updates changed how a hard file gets edited, from first cleanup to finished look.
  • It has been revealed that full disclosureThis article was brought to you by DxO.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A lot changed in DxO’s photo editing tools in 2026. The strongest noise reduction reached far more cameras. Masks learned to find each person in a frame, and the distance behind them, without a brush. The glow of film around a streetlight went from a stack of layers to a single filter.

Together, DxO’s software updates changed how a hard file gets edited, from first cleanup to finished look.

It has been revealed that full disclosureThis article was brought to you by DxO. DxO’s Black Friday prices apply to upcoming licenses and upgrades of PhotoLab 10, Nik Collection 9, ViewPoint 6, PureRAW 6 and FilmPack 8 through November 29. The prices are applied automatically at dxo.com/bf26/PetaPixel, with no code required.

Photos taken in Fresh Mexico by Chris Niccolls and Michael Bonocore, in Cuba and Morocco by Michael Bonocore, and the Milky Way by Matt Suess.

Recent findings suggest that dxO released new versions of four applications in 2026: PureRAW 6, Nik Collection 9, PhotoLab 10 and, in October, ViewPoint 6. DxO keeps improving its applications, and three of them received free updates in November.

Each one handles a different stage of an edit. PureRAW cleans the RAW file, the unprocessed data a camera’s sensor records. PhotoLab develops that file into a share-worthy photograph, ViewPoint corrects perspective and distortion, and Nik Collection adds the finishing look.

In a recent development, always looking for latest ways to edit old photos, I ran photos from New Mexico, Cuba and Morocco through three of them for PetaPixel stories throughout 2026. Even though I also shoot astrophotography, a fourth story followed OM SYSTEM ambassador Matt Suess through a Milky Way edit, as he is a much more impressive editor than I am. What follows runs in the order of a typical edit of mine, and that starts before any creative decision, with the RAW file itself.

If you zoom to 100% on a frame shot at a high ISO, the camera’s sensitivity setting, the flaws become obvious. There is grainy noise in the shadows, edges the lens left soft and a dust spot or two from the sensor. Every later editing adjustment that you add only makes the problems worse, and they follow the photograph through the rest of the edit.

In a recent development, pureRAW 6 helps to make all of these fixes. It applies noise reduction, lens corrections and dust removal to the RAW file before editing starts, then hands back a new file to edit. The usual choice for that file is a DNG, a format that keeps a RAW file’s editing flexibility. The original RAW file is never modified.

This year’s PureRAW 6 expanded the reach of DeepPRIME XD3, the stronger of PureRAW’s two noise reduction engines.

In the past, it only worked with Fujifilm’s X-Trans sensors. It now works with Bayer sensors, the design used by Canon, Nikon, Sony and OM SYSTEM.

Recent findings suggest that the lens corrections are an especially strong feature of DxO software, starting with PureRAW. They test each supported camera and lens pairing in their own lab, and PureRAW applies that impressive data for the exact combination that made the photograph.

Sources indicate that in this day and age with skyrocketing storage costs, PureRAW 6 shrinks the files with a latest DNG option called High-Fidelity Compression. In one example, a 57.8MB RAW file becomes a 136MB DNG without compression and a 17.2MB DNG with it.

I have come to find that most photographers are like me, and they often shoot with less than spotless equipment. Luckily, dust spots are automatically detected and removed across a whole batch. And in PureRAW 6, batch edits finish quicker, because the processor prepares the next image while the graphics card renders the current one.

It has been revealed that for noise reduction, start with DeepPRIME 3 and switch to XD3 for high-ISO files, heavy crops and fine detail such as feathers and fur. XD3 takes roughly twice as long, though the gap narrows on newer graphics cards, and it can leave artifacts (visible processing errors) on smooth surfaces. For portraits and architecture, stay with DeepPRIME 3.

If the processed file goes back to Lightroom, make sure to turn off its own lens corrections and noise reduction for that file. PureRAW has already applied both, and running them a second time doubles the correction and creates artifacts.

Industry observers note that pureRAW fits a photographer who plans to keep editing in Lightroom, Photoshop or Capture One, because it only changes the file those editors receive. A photographer who would rather work in one application gets DxO’s processing inside PhotoLab 10, the company’s all-in-one editor. The full walkthrough, with recommended starting values for each control, is in DxO PureRAW 6: The Ultimate Beginner’s Guide.

Brightening one face in a group photograph is a small change. Telling the software which pixels belong to that face is the slow part. The area an adjustment affects is called a mask, and building one by hand means painting an outline and then cleaning up its edges.

According to recent reports, photoLab 10 builds those masks itself, and my guide shows each one at work on my photographs from Morocco. Its AI Masks recognize the individual people in a photograph instead of treating the group as one subject. One easy step generates a separate mask for each selected person.

For portraits the masks go finer, selecting facial skin, eyes, teeth, lips or facial hair without a hand-painted outline.

In a recent development, no matter the subject matter, every photograph has depth, and the new Depth Masks select areas by how far they are from the camera. PhotoLab builds a depth map, a model of which parts of the scene are near and which are far, without needing depth data recorded in the file.

These masks utilize DxO’s own AI, which runs on the photographer’s own computer, so the masks work on an airplane or in a hotel with unreliable Wi-Fi. Additionally, for those concerned with privacy, this means that the photos are never sent to the cloud and stay local on their computer.

An automatic mask is a starting point to refine. When one misses part of the subject, PhotoLab 10 lets you correct it instead of rebuilding it.

Recent findings suggest that their U Point technology selects pixels by comparing their color and brightness. The Control Brush applies that matching inside an area the photographer paints.

Sources indicate that color grading shifts the color of the shadows, midtones and highlights separately. PhotoLab 10 puts all three on a single wheel, with a Global control for the whole image.

In a recent development, with the three ranges selected, dragging one marker moves all of them and keeps the same distance between them. This allows for trying a different color direction without rebuilding the color grade.

In a recent development, the free 10.3 enhancement, released in November, extends the masks to noise reduction. Each local adjustment, an edit confined to a masked area, can now use its own noise reduction engine. Reserve DeepPRIME XD3 for the subject, where it extracts the most detail, and let DeepPRIME 3 handle the rest of the frame.

Recent findings suggest that point a camera up at a building and its walls lean toward each other in the frame. That is a perspective problem, and no exposure or color control fixes it. ViewPoint 6 is the application to fix that: it corrects geometry, perspective and distortion.

Released in October, it adds AI masks to ReShape Fusion, the tool that reshapes part of a picture. A mask finds the outline of a subject, however complex its shape, and the correction mesh is built to match it.

According to recent reports, the photographer sets how far the change carries into the rest of the picture. As before, the correction needs no forced crop.

The standalone app now opens RAW files directly. November’s 6.1 update adds DNG export, so a RAW file corrected in ViewPoint can leave with its geometry fixed and continue in any editor that opens DNG files.

According to recent reports, saving and exporting are now separate. Save records the corrections for the next session, and Export produces the finished image.

In a recent development, photographers miss the days when film made bright lights glow. Light passed through the film’s layers, bounced off the back and leaked in again, leaving a soft halo around streetlights and candle flames. A digital sensor records the same lights with crisp edges and no halo.

Rebuilding that glow in Photoshop means duplicating the image, blurring the copy, masking the highlights and blending the layers together. Nik Collection 9 does it with one filter. The suite is a set of plug-ins for Photoshop, Lightroom Classic, Affinity and PhotoLab, and every application in the suite can open the photo from inside one of those editors.

In a recent development, that filter, Halation, is one of three newly introduced effects in version 9, each shown on my photographs from Cuba in my Nik Collection 9 guide. It works best on an image that already has strong highlights worth softening, such as a night cityscape or a backlit portrait.

Chromatic Shift copies the color offset of a misaligned printing press, the red edge on one side of a face and the blue-green shadow on the other. A subtle shift of that kind gives a portrait a retro, editorial feel. Using an AI mask can keep it off the eyes and lips.

Sources indicate that glass Effect distorts the frame as if it were shot through textured glass. On a portrait, the distortion can wrap the frame while an AI Object Mask keeps the face sharp.

In a recent development, the new Color Grading filter in Color Efex, one of the Nik Collection 9’s plug-ins, puts shadows, midtones, and highlights on one wheel. Two shortcuts move all three together: one shifts hue, the color the tones lean toward, and the other shifts saturation, how vivid that color is. It gives photographers who finish in Photoshop, Lightroom Classic or Affinity the single-wheel grading that PhotoLab 10 has built in.

In a recent development, eighteen blending modes now sit inside Color Efex and a second plug-in, Analog Efex. A blending mode sets how an effect mixes with the image beneath it. On the Halation filter, Multiply sinks the glow into the shadows for a darker image, while Soft Light keeps the glow and more of the original contrast.

Aim any of these effects at part of the frame with AI Object Masks and Depth Masks, which work in every plug-in.

Industry observers note that version 9.2, the November update, adds snapshots. A snapshot saves every edit made so far. Try a different look, then come back to the snapshot at any point in the session.

The revision also brings 18 latest presets, or saved looks: six each for Color Efex, Analog Efex and Silver Efex.

Matt Suess has photographed dark skies for decades and leads astrophotography workshops in places such as Grand Teton National Park. One of the most challenging files he has edited came from a test.

He normally caps his Milky Way exposures at ISO 6400, but he wanted to test PureRAW, so he shot a nightscape at ISO 12,800 to see how far he could push it.

In a recent development, sharpening or adding contrast to a noisy night file bakes the noise in, so Suess runs noise reduction before he develops the RAW file. He opens PureRAW’s Preview and Process mode, which reveals the controls first, because a night sky is where he wants to make those calls himself.

XD3 is the stronger engine, but a star field is where Suess often skips it. That much processing can start to soften the stars themselves, so he picks DeepPRIME 3, and he treats it as a per-image call.

He keeps Lens Sharpness on Standard, since the Hard setting starts sharpening the noise along with everything else.

The develop pass in Lightroom stays restrained. Suess switches to a color profile built for landscapes in place of the flatter default, adds a little contrast and holds back on the other sliders. He treats this pass as the place to protect the sky’s real color, with the finishing touches saved for later.

The finish happens in the Nik Collection 9 plug-in Color Efex, with the same four filters in the same order on nearly every Milky Way photograph. ClearView lifts the faint gray haze that dulls a night photo, and Suess keeps it low so it does not outline the stars. Glamour Glow spreads a soft bloom of light from the brightest points.

Remove Color Cast pulls one unwanted color out of the frame. Tonal Contrast raises contrast separately in the shadows, midtones and highlights, and he raises the midtones, where the structure of the Milky Way sits. Once the stack works, he saves it as a preset for the next photograph from his astrophotography session.

Suess fine tunes the filters with two tools. A Color Mask, a local adjustment added inside a filter, selects one color across the whole frame. He uses it on air glow, the faint green tint that indicates in the sky on very dark nights.

An AI Object Mask points a filter at a single foreground element instead of the whole image.

According to recent reports, he judges every move at 100%, not from the small preview. Each one gets a before and after comparison, and he looks for halos, the bright rings that too much contrast leaves around stars. Every step of the edit, with his settings, is in How to Turn a Flat, Noisy RAW Into a Finished Milky Way Photograph.

Some jobs cannot be done by developing a RAW file: a layered composite, added text, an object removed or replaced, detailed retouching. Those jobs need a pixel editor, software that changes the pixels of the picture directly.

DxO confirmed a partnership with Affinity by Canva in September. Affinity runs on macOS and Windows and costs nothing beyond a free Canva account.

According to recent reports, photoLab 10 introduced without a direct Export to Affinity button, and PhotoLab 10.1 added it. With the 10.3 revision, Affinity’s own .af files appear in PhotoLab’s library like JPEG and TIFF files.

That makes a round trip possible. A photographer can develop a RAW file in PhotoLab, continue in Affinity with retouching, compositing or layout, then finish and export the result in PhotoLab. Changes saved in Affinity are visible in PhotoLab straight away, and PhotoLab’s own adjustments are stored separately and never change the Affinity document.

Recent findings suggest that nik Collection 9.2 connects from the other side by saving its work as an .af file. The file keeps the edited image and the original as separate layers, and the masks come across as layers too. Going the other way has a limit: Nik Collection opens an .af file with its layers merged into a single image.

Sources indicate that dxO’s Black Friday prices cover upcoming licenses and upgrades of their five applications through November 29th, 2026. They apply to purchases from dxo.com/bf26/PetaPixel for macOS and Windows, are applied automatically with no code required, and cannot be combined with any other offers.

Sources indicate that pureRAW 6 suits a photographer who wants cleaner files and looks to keep editing in Lightroom, Photoshop or Capture One. It is $99.99, down from $139.99. The upgrade from version 4 or 5 is $69.99, down from $89.99.

PhotoLab 10 suits a photographer who wants one application for the whole edit, with DxO’s processing, the automatic masks and the Color Grading wheel in the same place. It is $199.99, down from $249.99. The upgrade from version 8 or 9 is $99.99, down from $129.99.

Nik Collection 9 suits a photographer who has an editor already and wants the finishing looks: film glow, color grading and blending modes without stacked layers. It is $149.99, down from $179.99. The upgrade from version 7 or 8 is $79.99, down from $99.99.

In a recent development, viewPoint 6 corrects geometry, perspective and distortion, and version 6, released in October, adds an AI mask that fits a correction to the outline of a subject. It is $99.99, down from $129.99. The upgrade from version 5 is $69.99, down from $84.99.

According to recent reports, filmPack 8 recreates the look of classic film stocks from laboratory measurements of real film, and it includes a tool that prepares home-scanned negatives and slides for editing. It is $74.99, down from $149.99. The upgrade from version 7 is $49.99, down from $89.99.

Free trials of every DxO application are available from dxo.com. November’s 10.3, 9.2 and 6.1 updates are free for owners of PhotoLab 10, Nik Collection 9 and ViewPoint 6.
