Sources indicate that feeling stressed? Whether you unwind with yoga or a relaxing massage, Thai massage combines the best of both worlds, benefiting your mind and body. Here’s everything you need to know!

Thai massage is a special kind of bodywork that blends relaxation with flexibility. Think of it as a gentle, full-body, more active experience. It’s all about boosting your flexibility and energizing your body. Just a heads-up: napping during a Thai massage might be a challenge!

Drawing from Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine, this ancient technique mixes assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and soothing rocking for 60 to 90 minutes. Unlike Western-style massages at a local spa, Thai massage takes place on a mat on the floor. A certified therapist will work to stretch your muscles and apply pressure along your body’s energy lines, known as sen, to release stress with a graceful, rhythmic touch.

You can schedule a Thai massage at many spas, massage clinics, and even some yoga studios, but make sure you find someone with the proper training and certification to give you an authentic experience.

In a recent development, when you arrive for a Thai massage, you might be given some comfy clothes, like a T-shirt and drawstring pants. You’ll remove your shoes, silence your phone, place your jewelry in a small dish, and settle onto a floor mat. Before the session, let the therapist know if you have any injuries.

If this is your first session, it can be intense, so focus on breathing and relaxing. You’ll likely start on your back, with the therapist beginning on your feet and legs. Since the therapist uses their body weight to guide you, it might initially feel a bit weird. Some discomfort is normal as your body stretches, but don’t hesitate to let your therapist know if anything feels uncomfortable.As the session progresses, you’ll likely switch positions, including flipping onto your belly or trying various other postures. Go with the flow as your therapist guides you through stretches and yoga-like moves designed to open up your joints, move your energy, and release tension. Keep breathing and communicate with your therapist throughout the process.

According to recent reports, as the session wraps up, you’ll enjoy some gentle rocking motions to ease you out of the massage. You might feel sore afterward, especially if it’s your first Thai massage, so hydrate and rest. You’ll likely feel incredibly relaxed, more flexible, and energized.

Preparing for a Thai massage is simple!

Pro tip: Clear your mind and be open to guidance. While the stretches may feel awkward initially, allow yourself to let go. This can help you fully experience the massage’s benefits.

Your Thai massage experience won’t resemble a Western-style deep tissue massage. You won’t be naked under a sheet on a raised massage table, and the massage therapist won’t be using long, deep strokes to work your muscles.The other significant difference is that, like some forms of yoga, Thai massage has a spiritual element based on Buddhism. As they use the weight of their bodies to work on your body, your therapist is also trained to send you kind, loving, healing vibes. The ultimate goal is to help you feel better by allowing your energy to flow throughout your body.

Industry observers note that the ancient practice of Thai massage combines assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and rhythmic rocking to unknot your body and get your inner energy flowing. Unlike Western massage techniques, you’ll be fully clothed on a floor mat, with the massage therapist using their entire body to release your tension.

Permit yourself to let go, and expect an active, sometimes intense, full-body experience that leaves you relaxed and energized.

MoMA PS1 Plans ‘Malvestir,’ Exhibition Looking at Latin American and Latinx Fashion and Contemporary Art

💡 Key Takeaways
  • MoMA PS1 in Latest York will open a major exhibition next spring looking at the connections between the spheres of Latin American and Latinx fashion and contemporary art.
  • Industry observers note that opening April 22, “Malvestir” will feature the work of 20 artists and designers, including Willy Chavarria, Camila Falquez, Carla Fernández, Bárbara Sánchez-Kane, Troy Montes Michie, Manauara Clandestina, and La Cholla Jackson, among others.
  • The exhibition’s title comes from a portmanteau with a long history that combines the prefix “mal-” (meaning poorly) and the verb “vestir” (to dress).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MoMA PS1 in Latest York will open a major exhibition next spring looking at the connections between the spheres of Latin American and Latinx fashion and contemporary art.

Industry observers note that opening April 22, “Malvestir” will feature the work of 20 artists and designers, including Willy Chavarria, Camila Falquez, Carla Fernández, Bárbara Sánchez-Kane, Troy Montes Michie, Manauara Clandestina, and La Cholla Jackson, among others. It will be curated by PS1 director Connie Butler and associate curator Elena Ketelsen González. Related Articles ARTnews Awards 2026 Established Artist of the Year: Vaginal Davis Have Fashion Folk Ruined the Frieze London Experience?

The exhibition’s title comes from a portmanteau with a long history that combines the prefix “mal-” (meaning poorly) and the verb “vestir” (to dress). Per a release, the “historical term [was] used in Spanish colonial dress codes that policed caste, race, and gender, labeling those who transgressed social boundaries or refused to comply as malvestidos.” While still a pejorative in contemporary Spanish, the release adds, that the term has been embraced as “a countercultural charge, as a deliberate rejection of Eurocentric taste and class decorum, or queer disobedience.”.

Sources indicate that art museums have increasingly embraced fashion exhibitions in recent years, at times pairing garments with contemporary art. PS1’s, however, was ahead of the curve: the institution exhibited fashion between 1980 and 1984 through its Multi-Disciplinary Program. The program was facilitated by the late Hollywood stylist and make-up artist Di Russo, who also served as its curator. Projects staged during the program’s run, including ones by Julio (1980), Homer Layne / Charles James (1981), Willi Smith (1982), and Betsey Johnson (1983), have been partially restaged for the museum’s current exhibition “New York Fashion at PS1, 1980–1984” (through March 15).

Among the pairings that will feature in “Malvestir” are the exaggerated proportions of Chavarria’s designs that draw from Chicanx fashion; the “Dominican-York” streetwear and queer nightlight fashions of LUAR; Falquez’s photographic portraits of queer and trans people; and Clandestina’s mixed-media installation TRANSCLANDESTINA 3020, which was commissioned for the 2025 Bienal de São Paulo.

Other themes that will be explored in the exhibition include the circulation and appropriation of Indigenous craft and aesthetics by Western designers and artists, Eurocentric notions of beauty standards and class aspirations, and the textile waste—called “pacas”—that is imported from the United States throughout Latin America.

“Over the past few years, we visited artists’ studios across the US, Central America, the Caribbean, and South America, and again and again we found artists and designers using the language of fashion to confront the commodification of identity, waste colonialism, and the pull of class aspirationalism,” Ketelsen González told ARTnews in an email. “Malvestir brings together some of the most exciting artists working today to show both the possibilities and the contradictions embedded in the politics of dress.”.

The full artist list follows below.

Industry News: In Sammy Baloji’s Hands, ‘Objective’ Materials Reveal Upcoming Truths About African History

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1215 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in the mid-2000s, after he completed his master’s degree in information sciences and communication at the University of Lubumbashi, Sammy Baloji started working with the French Institute.
  • Sources indicate that baloji’s work for the French Institute mainly entailed photographing events and later working with researchers from France.
  • In a recent development, working at the French Institute, he recalled in an interview with ARTnews, “really shifted my perspective, in terms of outlining photography or research, because I was interested in the way that [the researchers] were addressing the city or buildings or cultural heritage from a historical and objective perspective.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in the mid-2000s, after he completed his master’s degree in information sciences and communication at the University of Lubumbashi, Sammy Baloji started working with the French Institute. The director of the institute, also based in Lubumbashi, was interested in colonial architecture and cultural heritage history, and he collaborated with academics researching those topics.

Sources indicate that baloji’s work for the French Institute mainly entailed photographing events and later working with researchers from France. But he was already on the way to becoming the artist he is today. Related Articles Actor Says He Removed His Mother's Art from Venice Biennale Installation as a Pro-Israel Protest French Artist Claude Lévêque Ordered to Stand Trial for Rape and Sexual Assault of Minors.

In a recent development, working at the French Institute, he recalled in an interview with ARTnews, “really shifted my perspective, in terms of outlining photography or research, because I was interested in the way that [the researchers] were addressing the city or buildings or cultural heritage from a historical and objective perspective. I was mainly interested in people’s experiences, the testimonies of people who are living [in Lubumbashi like] myself.”.

The two opposite approaches opened up the question of how he could “use the so-called scientific objective materials and bring them close to the human experience, to the architecture of local sites.”.

The inquiry led the artist to make one of his first significant projects, Mémoire (2006), a photography collage series of colonial-era black and white archival images and colored prints showing contemporary Lubumbashi in the Katanga province, which is rich in mineral resources including copper, uranium, lithium, diamonds and cobalt.

Baloji’s work for the French Institute had allowed him to observe the social, environmental and political impact of mining in Katanga. Now, using a combination of photography and research, he was able to underscore how Belgian colonization had shaped the Democratic Republic of Congo, whose history of extraction he has continued to explore.

It has been revealed that works continuing to build on the themes of Mémoire can at the moment be seen in two high-profile showings. Baloji is making his debut US solo with “When Extraction Becomes Form It Speaks In Borrowed Tongues,” at the Wexner Center for the Arts in Columbus, Ohio, on view through February 14, 2027. The exhibition explores how Europe’s decorative arts and architecture still include elements of Congo’s colonialist history and the extraction of natural resources. It takes a critical look at the impact on land, people and cultural forms, speaking to complicated relationships between Central Africa, Europe, and the Americas.

Concurrently with the Wexner Center show, Baloji’s work can be seen at the Venice Biennale, both in the main show, curated by the late Koyo Kouoh, and in the national pavilion of the Democratic Republic of Congo. In the main exhibition at Venice, Baloji is showing three sculptures and 16 collage prints. Two of the sculptures reference works from a 19th-century Belgian colonial museum and the national collection built in the 1970s by the former President of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mobutu Sese Seko.

“I started to realize that the colonial system was not just about controlling territory but also occupying societies and imposing new rules,” noted Baloji, who splits his time between Brussels and Lubumbashi.

In the Wexner show, Baloji is exhibiting Suspension (Debris of History, Matters of Memory), a commission conceived with architect Gloria Cabral and in collaboration with art historian Cécile Fromont. Drawing from the design of historical Kongo cloth, the suspended large-scale sculpture is made of mining and construction waste, the latter from recent work at the Wexner Center. Meanwhile, a newly introduced tapestry called Rethreaded Indies, made by Baloji and Fromont, addresses the French Old Indies tapestry series (1637–1730), produced at the royal Gobelins manufactory in Paris, connecting that with Kongolese weaving. The works use textile and architecture to correct misinformation about African histories, showing how European colonization has shaped the continent’s narratives, often for the worse.

Industry observers note that “I would say my interest in his work is how he weaves these histories together, and in a way that I find extremely compelling,” mentioned Julieta González, the head of visual arts at the Wexner Center and the curator of the artist’s exhibition. Baloji’s work, she added, “is vital because it weaves together so many historical events and situations but with materiality that speaks to the particular situation he’s critiquing, which is the legacies of colonialism” in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The show she curated, she said, offers the public “an insight into [the artist’s] very research-oriented practice and how it unfolds in so many different mediums [which includes] video, sculpture and photography.”.

Sources indicate that baloji was born in 1978 in Lubumbashi and grew up with, in some sense, limited knowledge about the history of Belgium’s colonization of the Democratic Republic of Congo. (Connecting that and resource extraction in Katanga with global or political history came later following reports of Congo supplying Iran with uranium, which the Central African country denied.) In secondary school, Baloji cofounded a collective that read and shared books from libraries and schools that they had access to. He was also drawing at the time, producing some of his first artworks.

It has been revealed that his parents did not encourage his plan to study at the Fine Art Academy, so for his master’s degree, he studied information sciences and communication, which happened to align with the artistic practices he was interested in. Ironically, or maybe coincidentally, the course Baloji pursued to appease his parents so he could make his own career choices ended up being formative to his practice.

Industry observers note that baloji is also known for more than just his art. In 2008, he cofounded the Lubumbashi-based Picha Art and Research Center and the Lubumbashi Biennale, whose ninth edition, cocurated by Congolese-Belgian curator Sorana Munsya and Ethiopian-Eritrean-Italian artist Jermay Michael Gabriel, opened in October. The art space and biennial are platforms that help expand access to the arts and support local artists with needed infrastructure, especially because of limited state support.

Recent findings suggest that camille Ostermann, an independent art consultant who worked on Congo’s national pavilion at the Venice Biennale, said, “I’ve admired [Baloji’s] collaborative practice [since the early 2010s]: works co-authored with historians, exhibitions built around artists he invites. But it was at the Lubumbashi Biennale, which Picha organizes, that I saw this spirit at work. In a city shaped by mining, by what is extracted and carried elsewhere, Picha does the opposite: it builds, gathers, gives back. Many artists told me their paths had been changed by Picha and Sammy’s mentorship. Like Ibrahim Mahama in Tamale or Yinka Shonibare in Lagos, Sammy works internationally while staying rooted in Lubumbashi, deliberately keeping the two connected: what he builds abroad can open doors for others at home.”.

According to recent reports, picha Center and the Lubumbashi Biennale are also, in some ways, an extension of Baloji’s research and practice. The biennial, he stated, can start conversations about extractivism and ecological crisis, as well as talk about “the impact of international and economic interests on the environment and societies.” It was a statement that could easily have been applied to many of his artworks.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ron Howard knows his way around a camera: in front of and behind the lens; scripted film or documentary feature. But when his production company, Imagine Entertainment (co-chaired by Brian Grazer), was considering a biodoc on fashion photographer Richard Avedon, Howard wasn’t sure if he should be at the helm.

“I really went into it thinking, ‘This is a great subject, it’d be great for Imagine,’” Howard stated of the Avedon Foundation opening up the artist’s archives to him during a screening at SCAD Film Festival on Oct. 28. “As I began sort of seeing the breadth of that work, I was immediately impressed, but I still felt like, I’m not sure I’m really the right filmmaker for this, but this is fascinating and I bet we could explore what went on behind the scenes making many of these great photos that we remember.” Related Articles New Richard Avedon Documentary Shows That Fashion Isn't All Style--It's Substance, Too Netflix Acquires Richard Avedon Documentary for 2026 Release After Cannes Debut.

“As I began to do some research, soon I really did connect with it as this very human story that I wanted to tell,” Howard continued. “It was less anecdotal about how photos were done and what glamorous or intriguing figures sat for him, and much, much more about an artist’s journey, and I related to it. In some ways, we’re very different people—he’s an extrovert, I’m not; he was the life of the party, I avoid them—but, man, did he have drive and ambition.”.

In a recent development, the resulting film, Avedon, now streaming on Netflix, blends commentary from collaborators—former magazine editor Tina Brown, model Lauren Hutton and dancer and choreographer Twyla Tharp—with Richard’s works, both commercial and historic, like his portraits of figures of the civil rights movement. The project heavily explores Avedon’s legacy as an artist with strong creative and political convictions, as well as his struggle balancing those passions with his obligations as a husband and father.

Recent findings suggest that “Ultimately, we had 500 photographs in the documentary, but our amazing producing partner, Dallas Brennan Rexer, combed through 16,000 sittings of Avedon,” producer Sara Bernstein, president of Imagine Documentaries, explained during the Q&A. “Initially, we thought there might be a select number of hero images that would take us through Avedon’s creative story. But then there’s this backdrop of, essentially, the back half of the 20th century, so you could match these images with these different moments in history or these different personalities who represent different buckets of history. And then you were able to see a deeper, personal story when John Avedon sat down for us.”.

It has been revealed that richard’s son, John, whose son, Michael, is also a fashion photographer, was a “reluctant interview,” despite being supportive of the project, Howard noted as he shared how he got John on board as a talking head.“Frankly, I remarked to him, ‘There’s a gap here because we have your father’s voice. We have people who worked with him, but we don’t have that intimate connection, that deeper understanding that’s away from the studio.’ And I think as a writer himself, he recognized that there was a role for him to fill,” said Howard, later adding, “now [the film] became a generational thing about fathers and sons in addition to everything else.”In one of the final scenes of the film, Avedon, who died in 2001, makes a startlingly reticent prediction about the outlook on his art form, stating, “I don’t think there will be photography in the future, only machines.”Asked what he thinks Avedon would capture at this moment in time, where the battle between art and AI seems to be reaching its peak, Howard said, “He’d probably still be shooting on the white paper and probably still using that three-by-five camera because, for him, it did become a kind of communication and an exploration, capturing those moments. I think he would still be entirely relevant because he became the story behind the story as an artist. And we began to recognize his work; whether we knew it was Avedon, we could feel the hand of a creator.”.

Recent findings suggest that added Howard of how Richard might approach AI, “My guess is also with his sensibility and aesthetic, he’d be using it as a tool to advance his aesthetic. I don’t think he’d be necessarily running away from it, but he would want to stay in control.”.

The Best Booths at Frieze Abu Dhabi, From a Surrealist Take on the Iran-Iraq War to Mosaics

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From sales to the quality of works selling, Frieze Abu Dhabi is making a strong first impression.
  • Below, we’ve picked the eight best presentations at Frieze Abu Dhabi, which runs through Sunday, November 22.
  • Lebanese multidisciplinary artist Dala Nasser, 36, was the recipient of the inaugural 2026 Frieze Artist Award.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From sales to the quality of works selling, Frieze Abu Dhabi is making a strong first impression. A tight exhibitor list of 89 galleries has brought a selection of works that confront subjects ranging from war—something that the Middle East is no stranger to—to ideas of masculinity, memory, and religion. Much of the art on view goes beyond conventional painting, extending into life-size sculptures, mosaics and materials such as wood, metal and ink.

Below, we’ve picked the eight best presentations at Frieze Abu Dhabi, which runs through Sunday, November 22.

Lebanese multidisciplinary artist Dala Nasser, 36, was the recipient of the inaugural 2026 Frieze Artist Award. Fittingly, her installation, Qubbat Duris, is mounted in the center hall. The large-scale, sculptural installation is inspired by a 13th-century Ayyubid-era Muslim shrine found in Duris, a village in Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley, and has been rubbed with ash, raw clay and terracotta. More of Nasser’s works are on display at the Commonwealth and Council’s booth, albeit on a smaller scale. The fabrics here have been rubbed against ruins that are believed to be the burial sites of Noah, and bear natural dyes such as malachite, walnut, and madder, a reddish root frequently used in her practice. Nasser is known for her sculptural, stretched cloths, but the artist still considers herself a painter; this is her way of manipulating a canvas.

Thaddaeus Ropac’s booth includes to works by Imran Qureshi, each in different mediums. Water Bodies uses domestic water tanks commonly found in South Asia, onto which Qureshi applied broken South Punjab blue pottery, creating a mosaic. It’s a smart commentary on the craving for handmade but functional pieces within a mass-produced world; memories, it seems to say, are as easily discarded. Qureshi’s presentation features about 20 Mughal-inspired miniature paintings, which are in dialogue with the water tanks, united by colors and prints that speak to the horrors of war: one is decorated with a rocket, and a downpour of red paint—or blood.

Sources indicate that frieze Abu Dhabi opened under the shadow of the US and Israel’s war on Iran. Dastan Gallery’s, meanwhile, was dedicated to an earlier conflict: the Iran-Iraq War (1980-1988), which is the subject of Iranian artist Ali Akbar Sadeghi’s “Myth and Math” series. The painting are a Dalí-like interpretation of the conflict: heroes appear at war with themselves, in a Surreal setting. The booth traced the artist’s process producing the series, starting with sketches that include notes in Farsi reading “the eyes of the horses in the skeletons should be alive” and “the roots [of a tree] should be rooted in the sky,” among more. In one piece, Sadeghi symbolizes the horrors of war as a knight piercing a portrait that bleeds. Surprisingly, there’s hope, even if it’s a grain the viewer must search for in the blue color of the sky.

While overt depictions of sexuality may still be taboo in the UAE art scene, artists Hoda Tawakol and Zeinab Alhashemi, are elegantly addressing matters of womanhood.

Recent findings suggest that the Frieze Sculpture Park, located the shore of Saadiyat Island, holds Tawakol’s temple-like installation, Under the Sycamore Tree. A recreation of the Temple of Isis at Philae, in Egypt, the wooden structure displays a fabric inked with the silhouette of a sycamore tree; wings are suspended from its ceiling. “It’s a very fragmented vision of motherhood and a celebration of it in a world that is very gloomy right now with a lot of violence and wars,” Tawakol remarked, describing the pavilion as a shelter.

Sources indicate that A stone’s throw away is Alhashemi’s The Nut and Bolt, a large-scale (7 ft high, and 6 ft across) steel nut and bolt, with a blackened bronze patina finish, layered with meaning: the construction of Abu Dhabi into modern city; and Alhashemi’s experience of a 2009 car accident. The crash caused her thirteen bones fractures, some of which was reconstructed with metal. There’s phallic impression to the work too, with sex symbolized simply as a nut, bolt, and hole.

Industry observers note that “I can seem feminine in the nature of who I am,” Alhashemi noted, outfitted in a stylish abaya, Chanel bag, and Gucci shoes. However, she continued, “My ideas are quite brutal and masculine in their own way. I always tell myself that one day, hopefully, I will retire and be in a studio just painting flowers, and not being so specific on this kind of theme [masculinity]. To me, it’s important, it’s an expression.”.

Recent findings suggest that timothy Taylor’s solo presentation of the Los Angeles-based artist Hilary Pecis sold-out on the preview day of Frieze Abu Dhabi. The works center Los Angeles, drawing some parallels between Abu Dhabi—both cities are animated by nature with palm trees, blue skies and sandy beaches or islands—and more contrasts. Pecis’ paintings peek into their subject’s personal lives; domestic life in the Gulf remains a private affair. F.

Breakfast Table (2026) depicts morning routine: a pencil and sheet music on either side of a plate of sliced pineapple and a mug of coffee; a vase filled with hibiscus flowers and beside it, a globe. Vases (2026), a modernist still-life of vases filled with roses, poppies, and more floral arrangements, brought to mind a Jan van Huysum pendant painting of flowers and fruits.

The life of Lebanese-Armenian artist Seta Manoukian is Hollywood-worthy, or at least worth a memoir (it could be called “Art, Pray, Love”).

It has been revealed that the artist relocated to Los Angeles in 1985 after the Lebanese Civil War, painting war scenes and cityscapes. In the ’90s, she stumbled into a Buddhist monastery with a friend of hers, just out of curiosity. She found her calling. Manoukian took her Buddhist vows in 2005 and began a 10-year studio hiatus the following year. Marfa’ Projects, a Beirut gallery, is presenting one work from her pre-Buddhist life, Willing to Begin (1990), which depicts two men in suits and ties, separated by details taken from a Greek column. The surrounding works trace her journey as both a Buddhist and artist. Her transcendental paintings depict organic shapes, strands of hair and floating rocks. Prepare to Sweat (2018) shows a volcano erupting with a yellow rose, a symbol Manoukian indicates represent the start of the world.

Pace Gallery has dedicated its booth to a solo show of never-before-exhibited paintings by Aboriginal artist Emily Kam Kngwarray. It offers a moment for pause from the chaos of the fair. The artist was the subject of a recent retrospective at Tate Modern in July 2025 (running through this January). Her large-scale abstract paintings draws on cultural traditions, including Anmatyerr spirituality. According to Pace, she created on the paintings in Urapuntja—formerly known as Utopia—an Aboriginal Australian homeland, tracing root systems and life cycles of plants onto canvas. Kngwarray’s most striking works illustrate the wonders of the color orange, shapeshifting from a golden hue to an ashy purple.

Jordanian artist Ala Younis’ presentation at Taymour Grahne Projects draws on her former home in Abu Dhabi, a 1970s building decorated with mosaics, deep-set windows, and shaded balconies (a common architectural feature, given the region’s climate).

These buildings that have been overshadowed by Abu Dhabi’s new skyscrapers—turning them into relics, according to her series “Climate Conditions.” In it, Younis has recreated the structures in hand-cut stone mosaics from Jordan. The series gets its name from their construction: the building bear small cracks and spaces within their frame so they could naturally expand during the summer’s extreme heat, then decompress in the winter.

Recent findings suggest that looking at a cactus with its threatening spikes and tough skin, you might not immediately think, “Yep, that’s a thing I could eat.” But guess what? Some forms of cacti are edible, tasty, and quite good for you!

Check out why it might be a good idea to pal around with nopales, the pads of the prickly pear cactus.

It has been revealed that the nopal cactus, also known as the prickly pear or the opuntia, is a shrub-like, flowering cactus native to parts of Mexico, Arizona, the Mediterranean, Australia, and other desert regions. It might be recognized by its multitude of connected pads with flowering blooms. (A pad in bloom looks a little like a flat, green paw.).

Industry observers note that nopales flowers are filled with a viscous, seeded substance often used in jams, jellies, pies, cakes, and other sweets. But the stems, leaves, and entire pad (with spines removed, obvs) are also edible. Traditional Mexican preparations include boiling, grilling, and sautéing.

Science is still examining the possible benefits of nopales, so some touted wellness perks are fairly tentative. Here’s a look at what we know about these desert fruits.

Industry observers note that almost any time you see bright colors in edible fruits, it’s a sign they contain antioxidants. This is def true for Nopales!

According to recent reports, older studies have found that the fruit inside their flowers is rich in antioxidants like ascorbic acid, phenolics, and a mixture of betacyanin and betaxanthin. These compounds help fight inflammation by kicking harmful free radicals out of your cells.

Industry observers note that since they combat inflammation, the antioxidants in prickly pear could improve joint mobility. In a 2020 study, people who drank 3 ounces of prickly pear juice daily for 8 weeks had better range of motion and greater ease with daily activities than a control group who drank a placebo.

Research suggests nopales may help steady blood sugar. A 2014 study found that people with type 2 diabetes who ate nopales with a high-carb breakfast had significantly lower blood sugar and insulin levels compared to those who didn’t. However, this study only included 14 participants.

According to recent reports, in 2019, a larger systematic review assessed the fruit’s potential for blood sugar regulation. While it found insufficient evidence to support using nopales to reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes, the authors noted it might significantly reduce blood glucose levels.

Showing your liver some love might involve adding nopales (or a glass of nopal juice) to your diet. According to research from 2023, this has to do with prickly pear’s effects on triglycerides. By helping reduce triglyceride accumulation, nopales could relieve stress on the liver.

Industry observers note that whether you’ve overdone it on booze or are down with a stomach bug, it’s key to rehydrate with a drink that contains electrolytes. Consider prickly pear juice as your back-on-the-wagon beverage. It’s got potassium, magnesium, and calcium to help rebalance your electrolyte levels.

If you can track down fresh nopales where you live, cooking it yourself is a fun (if somewhat complicated) way to take advantage of its benefits. If not, look for prickly pear products, such as juices, being sure to check for added sugars.

Industry observers note that you can also take a supplement. Nopales supplements typically contain 500-650 milligrams (mg) per day.

While a prickly pear smoothie or nopales salad can be a healthy addition to your diet, consuming this cactus fruit may have some less-than-desirable side effects, like:.

If you’re fresh to nopales, take it slow at first to see how your body responds.

Sources indicate that don’t let the “prickly” in prickly pear keep you away from this desert gem. When prepared correctly, nopales are unique, nutritious food. Check ’em out when your fruit basket needs something a little different.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A Yoshitomo Nara painting sold for $15.9 million at Loïc Gouzer’s Fair Warning on Thursday, apparently making it the most expensive work by a living artist sold during Latest York’s busy auction week. Not bad for a sale with just one lot.

Recent findings suggest that in the Milky Lake / Thinking One (2011), an enormous painting of a young girl standing waist-deep in pale water, attracted four bidders from the US and Middle East before selling to an American buyer, according to a source familiar with the sale. It was Fair Warning’s 78 auction. Related Articles Christie's Notches a $145.9 M. Sale of 21st-Century Art, Led by a $32.9 M. Basquiat, amid Flagging Energy Led by Record-Breaking $190.4 M. van Gogh, Sotheby's Impressionist and Modern Art Sales Rake in $777.8 M.

Recent findings suggest that the result, just above its $10 million to $15 million estimate, is Nara’s third-highest price at auction, narrowly missing second place. His record remains the $24.9 million paid for Knife Behind Back (2000) at Sotheby’s Hong Kong in 2019.

Perhaps more surprisingly, Nara outperformed two of the biggest names in contemporary art. Jeff Koons’s Bob-Tail (1991) hammered for $9 million at Sotheby’s, while Gerhard Richter’s Abstraktes Bild (1991) brought in $9.4 million at Christie’s.

At 8.5 feet tall, the painting is the largest of Nara’s ever offered at auction, and the only major painting he completed in 2011, the year an earthquake and tsunami devastated northeastern Japan, where he grew up. The disaster had a profound impact on Nara’s work: his signature scowling children began giving way to quieter, more contemplative figures.

According to recent reports, the sale comes at a particularly busy moment for the Japanese artist. Earlier this month, David Zwirner opened Nara’s first exhibition with the gallery, filling two Chelsea spaces with paintings, drawings, and sculptures. Latest paintings are priced as high as $6 million, though the largest were being held for museums, according to a source familiar with the show.

Gouzer’s earned a reputation as a market whisperer when, in 2017, he helped clinch and sell Leonardo da Vinci’s Salvator Mundi for $450.3 million, still the most expensive work to ever sell at auction. Speaking to ARTnews ahead of the auction he pushed back against the idea that collectors had abandoned contemporary art in favor of established blue-chip names.

“Nara is as blue chip as it gets for contemporary art,” he stated, arguing that the artist’s relatively small output helps explain his market’s status.

Canva's 'AI off switch' finally recognises the backlash from creatives

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the past couple of years, most of the press releases coming from software companies have contained announcements of new AI features.
  • It has been revealed that canva is one of those companies, and it's introduced a bunch of generative AI tools to its design platform.
  • Canva has added two AI controls for both Free and Pro users.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the past couple of years, most of the press releases coming from software companies have contained announcements of new AI features. Image, video and vector generation, removal tools, agentic workflows, AI assistants, and myriad other advances that can help artists do in seconds something that used to take hours.

It has been revealed that canva is one of those companies, and it's introduced a bunch of generative AI tools to its design platform. So the email I received yesterday made me do a double take. On the day that Anthropic completed the world's biggest IPO in history, it introduced an 'AI off switch'.

Canva has added two AI controls for both Free and Pro users. The generative AI switch can be used to hide all of its generative AI tools, including Magic Write, Magic Design, Magic Expand, Dream Lab and Canva Code. It can be switched on or off at any time.

In a recent development, there's also an option to “See less AI content” on Canva's library of templates and design elements. This addresses complaints about the glut of AI-generated content making it harder to find quality work, something that's been causing problems on platforms as varied as Etsy and ArtStation.

Canva says AI-generated content remains a "small portion" of its library and that such content is identified in its metadata. Turning on the new function isn't guaranteed to remove it completely, but it should put human-made templates and design elements first in search results and recommendations.

The addition of a couple of toggles to the UI wouldn't normally be breaking news, so the fact that Canva feels this deserved its own announcement is telling. After heavily promoting AI tools, it's now presenting the ability to turn them off as a groundbreaking advance – and it is. This might be the first time that a major AI-forward creative software developer has recognised that a sizable portion of its user base just isn't into it.

"We believe AI has extraordinary potential to help people bring their ideas to life, and we're excited to keep pushing the boundaries of what's possible," Canva claims. "At the same time, like so many of you, we know there's something special about the time, care, and creativity that goes into making something that's truly yours.".

Industry observers note that an 'AI off button' is something that some creatives have been calling for. Part of the difficulty in implementing one is that it needs a definition of AI. Programs like Adobe's Photoshop have used machine learning for many years; it just wasn't branded as 'AI'. Many artists welcome tools that speed up their work, but not ones that do the creation part for them, especially if they're powered by models that were trained on unlicensed work.

Recent findings suggest that canva's recognised that. The toggle only turns off generative AI tools, such as ones that generate new imagery, text or code from prompts. Assistive editing tools like Background Remover or Magic Grab, which lets you select and move an object in an image will still be available. Using them won't cause your work to be shamed with metadata identifying it as AI-generated.

A 'no AI button' also requires a willingness from the provider. Since generative AI features are often charged on a per-use basis via credits, software companies generally want to encourage their customers to use them.

Adobe teased some impressive-looking AI-powered tools in the Adobe Max Sneaks presentation last week, but it's also clear that some customers detest generative AI, which has created a market for new tools like the artist-led Niva app, which is promoting itself as AI-free art software.

Will an AI-off button let Canva have its cake and eat it?

A French student who smashed a vitrine protecting the storied Stone of Destiny in Scotland noted he did so by right, claiming to having been born in Scotland and thus having been bestowed the privilege of sitting on a relic that had been used to crown Scottish monarchs until the 13th century.

It has been revealed that as reported by the BBC, “Arnaud Hercules Harixcalde Logan, 36, pleaded guilty to a charge of maliciously damaging the historic artefact’s glass casing at Perth Museum in July last year. Perth Sheriff Court was shown CCTV footage which demonstrated Logan using a blue and white hammer to strike the reinforced glass cabinet 24 times—causing £9,000 [around $12,000] worth of damage.”.

The incident, which forced the closure of the Stone of Destiny exhibit for three months, led to Logan being tackled by a museum visitor and a member of its staff. After an initial court appearance last year, the perpetrator fled to Australia and failed to check in with police for several months, as required by law. To that and the smashing incident, Logan pled guilty, with sentencing to follow on January 6.

It has been revealed that about the jarring day at the museum, a public prosecutor said, “Members of the public appeared distressed and panicked. Staff evacuated everyone from the building. He said he was called Logan and that the Logan clan had been betrayed and that the Stone of Destiny had been stolen from him.”.

Understanding your hair type is key to achieving healthy, luscious curls. Hair types range from 1 to 4 — straight, wavy, curly, and coily — with type 4 being the curliest. Type 4A hair has a fine texture and loose curl pattern, forming springy coils that need special care to stay healthy and vibrant.

Knowing your hair type helps determine the best hair care routine. Caring for 4A hair is essential, whether you’re dealing with dryness or breakage or want to define your curls.

Let’s dive into the world of 4A hair and discover how to keep those curls popping.

which refer to the width and density of your curls.

So, what’s the deal with 4A hair? 4A hair is the queen of the fine, loose curl pattern. It forms tight, springy coils that are like tiny, perfect S-shapes. These curls are less dense than their 4B and 4C cousins, making them more defined and delicate. Think of 4A hair as the Goldilocks of coily hair — not too tight, not too loose, but just right.

Industry observers note that your hair is unique and gorgeous, but it requires a bit of extra TLC to keep it looking its best. Here’s a straightforward guide to keeping your 4A hair moisturized, healthy, and thriving:.

In a recent development, 4A hair tends to be dry as its coily structure makes it difficult for natural oils to travel down the hair shaft. Keeping it moisturized is essential, so incorporate a good leave-in conditioner into your daily shampooing routine. Use deep conditioning treatments weekly to replenish moisture and strengthen your curls.

Industry observers note that don’t forget scalp care, too! For maximum hydration, look for products with ingredients like shea butter, coconut oil, and glycerin.

4A hair is prone to tangles, so detangle gently to avoid breakage. Use a wide-tooth comb or your fingers to work through knots carefully. Start from the ends and work your way up to the roots, and always detangle when your hair is wet and coated with conditioner to provide slip and minimize damage.

Heat styling tools can cause significant damage to 4A hair, leading to dryness, breakage, and loss of curl pattern. Minimize the use of blow dryers, flat irons, and curling wands. If you use heat, always apply a heat protectant spray first to shield your hair from high temperatures.

Pro tip: To maintain the health of your curls, opt for air-drying or styles that don’t require heat.

Protective styles like braids, twists, and buns can help reduce manipulation and minimize breakage. These styles tuck away your ends, protecting them from friction and environmental damage.

Cotton pillowcases cause friction, which leads to frizz and breakage, especially for 4A hair. Switching to satin or silk pillowcases instead helps mai.

ntain your curl pattern and prevent tangles.

It has been revealed that regular trims are crucial for keeping 4A hair healthy and preventing split ends from traveling up the hair shaft. Aim to trim your hair every 8-12 weeks to remove damaged ends and keep your curls looking fresh and vibrant.

To determine your hair type, look at the curl pattern, texture, and density. 4A hair has a loose curl pattern with fine, springy coils, while 4B and 4C hair have tighter curls. 3C hair is curly but not as tight as Type 4.

Industry observers note that washing once a week or every two weeks is generally sufficient for 4A hair. Overwashing can strip the hair of its natural oils.

Regular trims every 8-12 weeks help keep 4A hair healthy by removing split ends and preventing breakage.

Taking care of your 4A hair isn’t rocket science, but it does need a little know-how and the right tools.

Smiling for selfies should be fun, not painful! If cracked lip corners or angular cheilitis make it hard to smile, eat, or kiss, don’t worry. Check out these tips to heal those cracks quickly. With some care and good habits, you’ll have pain-free, makeout-ready lips in no time. Say goodbye to angular cheilitis and hello to a happier smile!

Sources indicate that the first step to healing your cracked lip corners swiftly is to lock in any moisture. Reach for a product dermatologists call an occlusive, which creates a protective barrier that prevents your lip corners from getting drier. Vaseline, Aquafor, or CeraVe ointment are common occlusives that will help reduce cracking.

Dab a little coconut oil, olive oil, or fragrance-free moisturizer on the corners of your lips daily after you shower. Make it a daily habit, but don’t go overboard. A little dab will do. Allow your skin’s natural oils to build back up as the cracking fades. Bonus tip: Add the occlusive lip barrier after moisturizing.

According to recent reports, locking in moisture only works if you have enough moisture, so staying hydrated is key! Keep a refillable water bottle with you as your trusty sidekick. Sip on plain water throughout the day, or jazz it up with a splash of cucumber or another non-acidic flavor. Pro tip: Avoid lemon juice, which can irritate and sting sensitive skin.

Bonus: Staying hydrated will help your raw lip corners heal quicker and improve your skin’s overall health.

Have you noticed that moisture is a common theme here? Lend your lips a humid hand by sleeping with a humidifier beside your bed. Adding moisture to the air is especially helpful for your cracked lips during the winter or in hot, dry climates. Think about popping a small humidifier in your workspace or wherever you spend the most time.

It has been revealed that it might seem like a quick fix to lick your lips to keep them moist, but that can make things worse. Saliva evaporates quickly, leaving a sticky residue that can attract bacteria and lead to infection. So, keep your tongue away from your lips and remember this: “Licking your lips will cause them to lickety-split.”.

Whether from frigid cold or dry heat, your skin can lose water rapidly, causing cracking, flaking, discoloration, or swelling. So avoid jumping from a sweltering afternoon at the beach into a freezing cold movie theater.

Also, skip the hot showers or cold plunges for a bit. These types of rapid temperature changes will rapidly dry out your lip corners. Bonus tip: Your lips can take a beating from the sun, so find a lip balm with SPF protection.

According to recent reports, if your cracked lip corners don’t improve or become especially painful or swollen in a few days, it’s time to visit a board-certified dermatologist. If left untreated, angular cheilitis can last for years, leaving your lips discolored or scarred.

Sources indicate that FYI: Angular cheilitis might not appear as clearly in people with darker skin. Instead of turning red, the affected skin may look pale and have a darker border.

It has been revealed that remember that lickety-split mantra? It’s for real. Saliva can get deposited in the corners of your lips for many reasons, like drooling, smoking, or sleeping with your mouth open due to some sniffles. Bacteria grows in those little saliva pools, triggering an inflammatory response that causes your lip corners to get irritated and crack.

Sources indicate that following these tips will make your lips feel better in about a week. Really bad cases of angular cheilitis can take a few weeks. Avoid smoking and eat a balanced diet to get faster results.

As mentioned above, Vaseline and other occlusives help create a protective barrier over the cracked lip corners, which helps the healing process.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Adobe software might still rule in many industries, but there's a growing number of alternatives, from Canva's free Affinity to open-source Krita, Maxon's Autograph for motion design and DaVinci Resolve for video editing.
  • Industry observers note that NIVA is clean and light, works in your browser and it's led by a conceptual artist rather than a software developer.
  • Industry observers note that like the recent AI-coded Adobe clones, NIVA was born out of a frustration with the direction of a certain Californian software giant.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Adobe software might still rule in many industries, but there's a growing number of alternatives, from Canva's free Affinity to open-source Krita, Maxon's Autograph for motion design and DaVinci Resolve for video editing. Into the fray, comes a new artist-led app who's main selling points include the fact that it DOESN'T have any generative AI tools.

Industry observers note that NIVA is clean and light, works in your browser and it's led by a conceptual artist rather than a software developer. After it was announced on Instagram this week, it picked up close to 30,000 users in 48 hours.

Industry observers note that like the recent AI-coded Adobe clones, NIVA was born out of a frustration with the direction of a certain Californian software giant. But it takes a very different approach. It wasn't vibe coded, and it doesn't attempt to replicate the look, feel or functions of any one existing program.

The project's led by Stuart Semple, an artist who previously annoyed Anish Kapoor by creating a very black shade of black.

"With Adobe pushing AI further into its tools, I wanted somewhere people could still practise their craft and make things themselves. No AI doing it for them," he says. "NIVA is very much our own thing that we've all built together.

Recent findings suggest that having previously made FREETONE, a free alternative to Pantone colours, with Culture Hustle, he started a Kickstarter for a project that was initially called Abode. He raised $240,000 from 3,000 backers, a few hundred of whom have been using the software regularly over a year and a half of beta testing. Around 10 people were involved more heavily in making the software, but Stuart states he largely built it himself "with help from some geeky friends from time to time when I've got stuck.".

At some point the name changed, and the project became NIVA. "I can't say I woke up to a nasty letter from the lawyers representing Adobe for legal reasons, so I won't," Stuart comments.

NIVA has many of the core tools and functionalities of a program like Photoshop. There are brushes, a pen tool with boolean ops, cloning and healing tools, layers, curve adjustments and blend modes, type tools with kerning, layouts and gradients.

Recent findings suggest that but it's lighter, with a more minimalist UI and fewer menus despite providing the ability to draw vectors, manipulate photos and lay out text and pages all in a single app. Owners also get a portfolio page, and there's a visual asset library called Storehouse, where you can store, sort, search and share work. Work can be exported in formats including PDF and SVG.

The pricing model is refreshing too. There's no subscription, and NIVA is free to use for an hour a day. You can buy full-day passes for $10 a time, or you can buy permanent access for $100. If you buy a day pass and later go permanent, the price of the day pass will be discounted. This allows a full opportunity to try the software before committing.

The response so far has been more enthusiastic than Stuart ever imagined. "I'm so excited and a bit freaked out", he admits, adding that what he finds most encouraging is that over half of the people who used NIVA in those first 48 hours made something with it within 40 seconds of getting access.

According to recent reports, "We're finally at a stage where it's stable enough and good enough to share with the world," he adds. It's only version one, the start of something I hope will be great. I still have loads I want to do with it".

You can use the software online at NIVA.design.

Breaking: What Does Dark Green Poop Mean? Causes, Diet, and When to See a Doctor

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bum nuggets typically sport a classic brown, so glancing back into the loo and spying on greenish-colored poop can throw you for a loop.
  • It has been revealed that most of the time, green poop reflects a leafy diet or your body’s unique way of breaking things down.
  • Continue reading to learn more about poop color, its meaning, and when it’s time to make an appointment with a healthcare provider.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bum nuggets typically sport a classic brown, so glancing back into the loo and spying on greenish-colored poop can throw you for a loop.

It has been revealed that most of the time, green poop reflects a leafy diet or your body’s unique way of breaking things down. But if the green becomes a recurring (fecal) matter, it might be something else.

Continue reading to learn more about poop color, its meaning, and when it’s time to make an appointment with a healthcare provider.

Spotting green or another unexpected color in the toilet can be startling, but it’s more common than you might think. From dietary influences to your body’s digestion speed, several factors can change poop from earthy tones to other shades. Let’s check some out.

Are you chowing down on lots of green leafy veggies like spinach, kale, or broccoli? These foods are high in chlorophyll, which can dye your doodles green. Chlorophyll doesn’t always break down entirely before reaching your intestines, meaning it passes through your system and colors your stool green.

In a recent development, have you ever had a St. Paddy’s Day-themed milkshake or a brightly colored cake? Artificial colors in foods and drinks can change poop from brown to green. It’s not magic! It’s just the dye in green food passing through your gut unchanged.

When your digestive system processes food too rapidly, it doesn’t allow for the full breakdown of bile, a yellow-green fluid that aids digestion. This often results in a greenish stool, especially during fast-moving episodes of diarrhea.

Sources indicate that have you recently been taking antibiotics? These meds can reset your gut’s bacterial crew. Since these tiny critters play a massive part in the shade of your stool, introducing antibiotics might cause green poop sometimes.

Sources indicate that if you’ve had certain medical treatments, it can affect digestion and cause bright green poop. One example is graft-versus-host disease, which may occur with bone marrow transplants. This tricky condition can bring about less-than-welcome guests, like diarrhea and green stool. It’s a clear signal from your body that things are out of sync.

In a recent development, some uninvited microscopic guests like Salmonella bacteria, the water-loving mini parasite Giardia, and norovirus can also be a reason for your poop turning green. These critters can hustle your digestion at an unnaturally quick pace, turning your stool green as they disrupt your gut’s usual rhythm.

Babies can surprise you with a whole crayon box of poop colors, and green is definitely in the mix.

According to recent reports, for infants, green stool might stem from the same factors as adults, like dietary changes. This includes adjustments when they start eating solids or changes in a parent’s diet if chestfeeding.

Recent findings suggest that another harmless cause could be ingesting a small amount of amniotic fluid in the womb. So, if you notice your little one sporting some spring grass-colored diapers, it’s usually no biggie.

If the green theme park in your toilet isn’t closing down, or if it’s accompanied by other symptoms like severe stomach pain, nausea, or diarrhea, it might be time to call in the pros. Persistent changes in stool color may signal underlying health issues that need medical attention.

Industry observers note that dark green poop can result from eating lots of leafy greens or foods with green coloring. However, it can also indicate that food travels rapidly through the digestive system.

While liver issues can change stool color, they usually turn it pale or dark, not green. If you’re worried about liver health, look for pale or clay-colored stools instead.

If you haven’t been on a kale-eating spree, dark green poop might be from iron supplements or constipation remedies, which can also give poop a greenish tint.

Sources indicate that dark poop could be a sign of your diet or medications. However, if it’s black and tar-like, it might mean bleeding in your upper gastrointestinal tract. In that case, chatting with a healthcare professional is a must.

It has been revealed that while green poop can def throw you through a loop, it’s usually not a sign of anything serious. It’s often your body’s way of dealing with what you eat or how fast you digest. So, unless it’s paired with other worrying symptoms, there’s probably no need to panic.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best environmental storytelling in video games doesn’t always hit you in the face and demand you stop to look, and GTA 6 has perfected that.
  • Rockstar’s developers say that kind of discovery is central to Grand Theft Auto 6, a world designed to reward players who take their time.
  • “The life is in the detail of Grand Theft Auto VI,” notes Adam Cochrane, Vice President of Art: Environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best environmental storytelling in video games doesn’t always hit you in the face and demand you stop to look, and GTA 6 has perfected that. Sometimes it’s a carefully dressed room, an overgrown garden, or a detail you spot out of the corner of your eye while heading somewhere else.

Rockstar’s developers say that kind of discovery is central to Grand Theft Auto 6, a world designed to reward players who take their time. After three weeks of playing GTA 6, I'd say the world-building is some of the best, most detailed, and most nuanced I've experienced. It can be as small as mud on a character's trainers, a branded coffee mug, or a car decal.

“The life is in the detail of Grand Theft Auto VI,” notes Adam Cochrane, Vice President of Art: Environment. “The subtle sway of trees or bunting swaying in the wind. A puddle of bin juice around the bottom of a dumpster, or an overgrown garden in a property that is unoccupied.”.

It’s the sort of detail that makes a place feel inhabited rather than assembled for a game. Cochrane points to the personalisation of homes and businesses, and the little vignettes the teams have added for players to discover. Some offer in-game rewards; others are there simply to be found.

According to recent reports, “Then you zoom out, and you look at the sheer scale of the world, and you realise that the detail you’ve been discovering on such a small scale is quite literally everywhere across the vast landscape of this world,” he indicates. “Then you realise that it’s all been curated, considered, and created by a human hand, and you can’t quite believe it.”.

That thinking extends beyond what you can see. Steven Messinger, Senior Design Director: Open World, explains that Rockstar has built deep backstories for things players may only glimpse. The game’s gang compounds, for example, have a fully mapped drug network, from supply routes to street-level buyers.

“Players will only pick up on bits and pieces of this,” Messinger notes, “but having that structure in the background as something we consistently refer to helps everything feel more real, like this big machine is always running even when players aren’t there.”.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a huge amount of work for details many players may miss. That’s rather the point.

Industry News: Cotswolds barn renovation by ConForm creates a "dialogue between old and latest"

💡 Key Takeaways
  • London studio ConForm Architects has transformed a former cattle barn into a multifunctional space for a working farm in the Cotswolds, contrasting its original red-brick and timber structure with zinc and black-timber additions.
  • Named Open Byre, the 124-square-metre barn has been adapted into a flexible space for meetings and gatherings, with the first floor containing a standalone apartment for guests.
  • ConForm Architects‘ design responds to the dual nature of the barn’s surroundings – with traditional red-brick farm structures to the east and more contemporary agricultural barns to the east – combining restoration with a new contrasting palette of stone, metal and timber.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Rory Gaylor.

London studio ConForm Architects has transformed a former cattle barn into a multifunctional space for a working farm in the Cotswolds, contrasting its original red-brick and timber structure with zinc and black-timber additions.

Named Open Byre, the 124-square-metre barn has been adapted into a flexible space for meetings and gatherings, with the first floor containing a standalone apartment for guests.

ConForm Architects‘ design responds to the dual nature of the barn’s surroundings – with traditional red-brick farm structures to the east and more contemporary agricultural barns to the east – combining restoration with a new contrasting palette of stone, metal and timber.

It has been revealed that “The design centres on a dialogue between old and newly introduced. Rather than blending the interventions into the existing fabric, we wanted each to remain legible and reinforce the other,” studio partner Ben Edgley told Dezeen.

“The building sits between two distinct parts of the farm: the older red brick buildings around the formal front farmyard and the more recent, industrial agricultural structures beyond,” he added.

“The design responds to both, retaining the brickwork and slate roof at the front while using zinc and blackened timber at the rear to reference the newer farm buildings.”.

A defining feature of the barn’s fresh rear facade is a projecting volume wrapped by gabion walls, filled with locally-quarried stone and punctured by a large window illuminating a cross-laminated timber (CLT) staircase.

In the ground floor’s flexible office and arts spaces, the idea of material contrasts continues, with original red-brick walls and repaired timber ceilings accompanied by joinery including desks, storage and a bathroom pod in black through-coloured MDF.

Above, the guest apartment is tucked beneath the exposed beams of the barn’s roof, with its own dedicated living room, kitchen-diner and bathroom finished in matching black timber.

“The central CLT stair is the defining gesture. It brings together structure, circulation and spatial organisation, drawing the eye from the entrance through the building towards the trees beyond,” said Edgley.

“Its scale and material presence establish a clear contrast with the existing brickwork and timber frame,” he added.

“The clients were closely involved in the process, undertaking much of the timber repair alongside local craftsmen. Their commitment to retaining the original fabric was central to the project.”.

ConForm Architects was founded in 2017 by Edgley alongside Eoin O’Leary.

Previous projects by the studio include a terraced home in London with perforated metal floors to filter daylight and a green-terrazzo flat extension modelled on bay windows.

Photography by Rory Gaylor.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The sun sign is the *it girlie* of the “significant three” elements in astrology.

But do you know about your moon sign and rising sign?

We chatted with an astrologer to understand what they are and how to calculate them.

According to Olga Verkhotina — astrologer and personal coach — the big three in astrology are your three most significant chart elements:.

“While a natal chart contains so many more intricate details beyond just three elements, the substantial three is a way to determine the main highlights that make up your personality and overall temperament,” Verkhotina states.

Verkhotina explains that a rising sign is the zodiac sign that falls at the beginning of your First House — basically, the beginning of your natal chart.

“The First House in astrology is associated with a person’s identity, individual activity, even their appearance, and the sign that houses that theme gives its characteristics,” she notes.

“Knowing your rising sign describes the way others may perceive you, the way your behavior comes across, as well as how you approach new situations in life.”.

You’ll need: date, time and place of birth.

“Knowing the accurate time is key here because even 10 minutes can make a difference in the sign,” Verkhotina explains.

In a recent development, “Once you have the data, you can trust astrology software to calculate it for you. There are a lot of natal chart calculators online, so you can just search ‘rising sign calculator,'” Verkhotina states.

Pro tip: Verkhotina suggests reading horoscopes from your rising sign instead of your sun sign, saying it will likely give more personalized insights on which areas of your life might be impacted by current cosmic events.

“A moon sign describes the position of the moon on the zodiac wheel at the moment of your birth,” Verkhotina states.

She explains that the moon in astrology symbolizes:.

“The moon sign helps you better understand how these themes demonstrate themselves in your life,” Verkhotina claims.

Unlike the rising sign, you don’t have to have the precise time of birth to know your moon sign, although Verkhotina indicates it’s still recommended.

You can also use an online calculator to find your moon sign or refer to the ephemeris — a table showing the daily positions of planets.

Verkhotina describes the sun sign as the most important planet in your chart.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s the center of your vitality, your ego, consciousness, and individuality at its core. That’s why it’s the most commonly known element in astrology,” she says.

It represents the zodiac sign the sun was in at the time of your birth, which Verkhotina says gives your individuality certain qualities associated with its specific sign.

“It’s important to understand that although the sun is a huge element in astrology, it doesn’t cover the nuances of one’s character,” Verkhotina explains.

Instead, she notes it just represents overall traits.

Verkhotina adds that the specifics of your character are covered in the rest of your astrological chart. “This is why sometimes no two leos are the same,” she notes.

This one is easy peasy — you don’t have to have your time or place of birth.

Sources indicate that “The sun cycle is very similar every year, so you can look it up by the date, month and year of your birth. Each sign corresponds to a calendar date that year,” Verkhotina claims.

Here’s each astro sign, in a nutshell, according to Verkhotina.

Your sun sign is important, but your moon and rising signs add extra details.

Your rising sign reflects your identity and how others see you, while your moon sign reveals your emotions and behavior.

To find these signs, you can use online birth chart calculators. Just make sure you have your birth date and time handy for accurate results.

Industry observers note that I test out the very best audiophile wired headphones for a living and out of all of them, the best open-back option is hands down the HEDDphone D1. And even at its original price of £599, it's worth every penny.

But thanks to this early Black Friday headphone deal, the HEDDphone D1 is now down from £599 to £499 over at Peter Tyson.

Industry observers note that open-back headphones are the holy grail for audiophiles craving a spacious soundstage, but they usually offer some unique hurdles to achieve true tonal accuracy. When I first heard the HEDDphone D1 last November, I noted that the German audio company had cracked the code. It's why they remain my top pick of the best-sounding wired, over-ear headphones at any price.

Sure, the HEDDphone D1 pack world-first driver technology and are hand-built in Germany, but for me that's not the main pull. It's the sound these things make! If you want neutral, balanced, slightly lean and mean but with exquisite detail, they're the best option at £599 – and a steal at £499!

It has been revealed that if you do get the HEDDphone D1 it's worth getting a quality headphone stand too. And you really don't have to spend loads of money to get a good-quality, handsome, wooden stand. For me a good option is the Linkidea wooden stand. Even when it's not discounted, under £30 is a bargain.

Usually I don't pay the marketing hype much time, but I make an exception with the HEDDphone D1. That's because they offer the world’s first dynamic driver headphone with a Thin-Ply Carbon Diaphragm (TPCD). Developed in partnership with Swedish material specialists Composite Sound, this aerospace-grade tech controls resonance structurally, eliminating the need for normal driver damping (and the compromises that that method invariably brings). What that all means for me and you is fast transients, and excellent clarity. These things are detailed!

Recent findings suggest that at 350g, they are lightweight for this tier of headphone – audiophile headphones can get heavy at around the £500 mark. With an impedance of 32ohms and 100dB sensitivity, they're easy to drive – including with inexpensive dongle DACs.

This is a genuinely special headphone, and a decent Black Friday price.

Sources indicate that lavera Grace is a watercolour artist from Australia who has always felt drawn to magical stories and the natural world. She states that inky lines and layered watercolours feel the most natural medium to achieve this, allowing ideas to flow onto the paper.

Below, Lavera briefly presents four examples of her work. If you're inspired and need supplies for your own work, see our guides to the best watercolour paints and the best watercolour pencils. We also have a selection of watercolour tutorials.

“Inspired by the fairy tale, The Frog Prince, I had an idea to tell the story in the faerie kingdom. I wanted to depict this encounter as a moment of enchantment between two characters.”.

It has been revealed that “The Twilight films inspired the atmosphere and colour palette of this painting. I wanted it to feel cold, at that magical time of evening right before dark, beneath a bright full moon.”.

“I created this artwork during a phase of obsessive reading. After struggling to find inspiration and wishing to be back in my books, the concept for this piece emerged organically.”.

“I used my subject matter to create a border for the scene. I’ve recently been inspired to experiment more with shape and design; to not always have my compositions so confined within borders.”.

You can see Lavera's work in progress on her YouTube channel.

Yoga and Overweight: Health Benefits and Tips for Getting Started

📅 31 Aug 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (763 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that part of the beauty of yoga is its accessibility for everyone.
  • It has been revealed that for wellness, you’d be hard-pressed to find a more holistic practice than yoga.
  • The limb-stretching, muscle-engaging, bodyweight-bearing nature of yoga has many physical benefits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that part of the beauty of yoga is its accessibility for everyone. Yoga practitioners come in all shapes and sizes and are hella modifiable. If you have overweight, there’s 100% a place for you in the world of downward dogs, crescent lunges, and resting pigeons.

Check out these benefits of yoga for overweight.

It has been revealed that for wellness, you’d be hard-pressed to find a more holistic practice than yoga. Your physical and mental health can get a boost from busting out your mat.

The limb-stretching, muscle-engaging, bodyweight-bearing nature of yoga has many physical benefits.

For starters, yoga may enhance your metabolism. An older study found that people who practiced had greater metabolic efficiency and lower weight than non-yogis.

It’s clear, too, that yoga’s combo of cardio and strength torches calories. A 160-pound person can burn around 180 calories per hour, popping in and out of poses. A 2021 study revealed that both Hatha and vinyasa yoga led to weight loss, with an average of 3.4 kilograms (7.5 pounds) lost over a 6-month.

Extra strength and flexibility are two other well-known upsides of the practice. Research shows that even sedentary folks can build these elements of fitness by taking up yoga. One study indicated that, after 8 weeks of practicing at least twice a week (180 minutes), people with no prior yoga experience had greater muscle strength, endurance, flexibility, and cardio-respiratory fitness.

According to recent reports, on the surface, yoga might look like mere stretching — but the practice goes far beyond the physical. Yoga engages the mind in all sorts of ways that may have benefits for overweight.

According to recent reports, by training your brain toward calm and focus, yoga sessions encourage mindfulness. A mindful outlook can have far-reaching effects in multiple areas of life, like promoting mindful eating and greater body awareness.

As a form of self-care, yoga can also promote a healthier body image. In a 2018 study, young adults who made it a habit reported higher satisfaction levels with their bodies. Better self-esteem and motivation have also been linked to the practice.

According to recent reports, then, too, yoga’s stress-relieving effects might follow you off the mat and into the dining room. Some research has found that people who do yoga binge eat less often.

Industry observers note that wanna get started with yoga but aren’t sure how? We got you.

It all starts with setting realistic goals and expectations. If you’ve never practiced before, you won’t be pretzel-ing yourself into challenging poses like scorpion or crow overnight — and that’s OK. Consider setting smaller, step-wise goals, such as attending a 30-minute class twice a week or mastering a few basic poses. Little by little, you’ll work your way up to a more advanced practice.

It’s also wise to select a class (or video) for beginners. Check your gym or yoga studio’s schedule for introductory sessions, and don’t be afraid to let an instructor know before class that you may need some modifications. Most are happy to provide adaptations to make the class a better experience for beginners.

Meanwhile, if you’re pursuing a yoga practice for weight loss, remember to pair it with other healthy lifestyle practices for best results. Though stretching and holding poses burn calories, yoga might not take you to your weight loss goal alone. A balanced diet, cardio exercise, and sufficient sleep are other keys to achieving a healthy weight.

Industry observers note that yoga stereotypes of scantily clad gym babes in impossible contortions might make you feel somewhat intimidated about in-person classes. If you’re concerned that a gym session will make you self-conscious, start with an at-home practice. (YouTube is a treasure trove of classes and instructors explicitly geared for people with overweight.) All by yourself in your living room, there’s no one to impress.

Industry observers note that or, if you’re up for in-person yoga, let your instructor know your needs again. Modifications are always possible.

No matter where you practice, credit yourself for showing up for your health. And, at the beginning of your session, don’t forget to set an intention you find motivating or encouraging, such as “I am caring for my body” or “I am worthy of love and respect.”.

Overweight doesn’t have to be a barrier to taking up yoga. Start small, knowing that you’ll get more comfortable with each session. With all the physical and mental health benefits a yoga practice provides — and all the modifications that make it more accessible — it’s worth a try, regardless of weight.

💡 Key Takeaways
