  • The small building stands on a one-acre site in Wilson, Wyoming, located just beyond the popular ski town of Jackson.
  • Before the project’s inception, the clients had lived on the property for 25 years – in a modest, 1960s house they had renovated – and had raised their son there.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Matthew Millman.

US studio CLB Architects has completed an accessory dwelling unit called Wiley, which features an outdoor climbing wall and compact living quarters for an empty-nester couple.

The small building stands on a one-acre site in Wilson, Wyoming, located just beyond the popular ski town of Jackson. The site is dotted with mature trees and sits along the west bank of the Snake River.

Before the project’s inception, the clients had lived on the property for 25 years – in a modest, 1960s house they had renovated – and had raised their son there.

As their son neared graduation from high school, the couple decided to build an ADU on the property and make it their full-time residence, while renting out the main residence.

“The new house would allow them to remain on the land they had known for decades, while experiencing it in a new way – closer to nature, with stronger connections to light, views and outdoor living,” mentioned Jackson-based CLB Architects.

The house also represents a way to accommodate a growing need for housing while preserving the natural landscape.

“In our region, there’s a clear need for this housing type, which is economical, compact and responsive to place,” said CLB Architects partner Eric Logan.

A primary challenge for the design team was to ensure the house “met the couple’s programmatic and budget constraints” within a very compact footprint. Per country regulations, the upcoming house could not exceed 1,000 square feet (92.9 square metres).

The architects conceived a simple, rectangular volume that rises two levels and is topped with a gabled roof. The house was carefully sited so it would feel separate from the main residence.

“Siting the building toward the back of the parcel and introducing fresh landscaping and tree plantings created a soft buffer between the two dwellings,” the architect said.

According to recent reports, the team carved out portions of the exterior to form inset terraces, along with a climbing wall that is used by the couple’s son while home from college. On the east-facing elevation, a boxy protrusion forms a balcony.

According to recent reports, both inside and out, the team opted for materials that were durable, cost-efficient and complemented the building’s form. Dark corrugated metal clads most of the building, while tight-knot cedar was used for inset areas to provide “warmth and depth”.

The ground level contains a spacious garage for vehicles and outdoor gear. The upper level holds two bedrooms with ensuite bathrooms, all of which are organised around a central living area.

“Locating the main living spaces on the second floor allows the interiors to engage the tree canopy while maximising natural light, offering a more intimate relationship with the landscape,” the team said.

The living area opens onto a west-facing deck, which acts as an “outdoor living room” for much of the year. Large, sliding glass doors diminish the boundary between inside and out and usher in breezes during summer months.

Sources indicate that the clients, both of whom have deep experience in design and construction fields, poured themselves into the project. The husband served as the general contractor and engaged local tradespeople to help out.

“A true labor of love, the couple built much of the house themselves, working on the construction every evening and on weekends,” the team noted, noting the project was completed in about nine months.

The project offers ideas for how communities in the Mountain West can accommodate growth while preserving the natural landscape.

“With rising land values and the need to accommodate more residents, homes like this – that are compact, efficient, and contextual – can provide more housing while preserving open space,” the team said.

“As local communities grapple with growth, projects like this suggest one path forward.”.

Other ADUs in America include a small, cedar-clad dwelling in California’s wine country by Schwartz and Architecture, and a compact, metal-clad building in Austin by North Arrow Studio that resembles a birdhouse.

These 8BitDo Tomb Raider controllers have made me rethink collectable gaming hardware

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I've never really been one for collectable controllers.
  • Sources indicate that this is proper packaging design, crafted as much for the fan experience as for protecting the controller.
  • The controller sits on a sliding shelf, so even getting it out is part of the experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I've never really been one for collectable controllers. I'm a fairly practical gamer, I suppose, and while I appreciate nice hardware design, I'm usually more interested in how a controller feels than how it looks, whether it has an on-brand D-pad or decals, for example. But opening the Tomb Raider 30th Anniversary Edition of 8BitDo's Ultimate 3 Controller has changed my mind a little, and I think it's largely down to the box.

Sources indicate that this is proper packaging design, crafted as much for the fan experience as for protecting the controller. The Ultimate 3's box changes shape, opens, slides and reveals its secrets, almost like Lara Croft discovering some long-lost treasure, and I found myself enjoying the whole process far more than I expected. There's even a little golden envelope, almost hidden away, containing the instructions and a month of Xbox Game Pass Ultimate. It's all very Tomb Raider, and yes, I know I'm getting excited about a cardboard box.

The controller sits on a sliding shelf, so even getting it out is part of the experience. Then you start noticing the little design details. The faded brown-and-gold colourway features Lara silhouettes across it; there's a lovely golden metallic D-pad, and the whole thing looks like something recovered from an ancient tomb. The D-pad itself reminds me of a lost coin or compass face, which is a nice touch.

Recent findings suggest that the metal D-pad disc did fall off once, but clipped back in fine. Do I expect that from a $120 controller? No, not really. Do I expect it from a $120 collectable controller where brand and design dominate? Yeah, probably.

In a recent development, I like that 8BitDo hasn't gone overboard with the branding; it feels like a well-made piece of gaming hardware, with the Tomb Raider design integrated rather than simply plastered on. The buttons are solid black, the sticks feel responsive, and the controller has a reassuring weight. The triggers have a nice solid feel, not too light but with a little flick as they snap back into place if released.

Then there's the stand, which I think is my favourite bit. The controller sits snugly in place, with a matching decal underneath, and it looks like you're slotting an ancient stone artefact into some sort of polar key and lock from the games. A soft orange LED glows when the controller charges, and suddenly I've got a little Tomb Raider shrine on my desk. I didn't think I needed one, but here we are.

Sources indicate that what's clever about the design is that it gets at the look and feel of Tomb Raider without relying on Lara's face everywhere. The original games had such a distinctive visual identity: those angular environments, sandstone ruins, green foliage and Lara's turquoise costume, and it's a look that's stuck with me. The Ultimate 3 is more of a celebration of Lara across the series, but the colours, materials and little relic-like details bring back some of that atmosphere.

The less expensive Pro 3 Bluetooth Gamepad takes a more direct route back to the original game. Its design is inspired by the Lost Valley, with a jungle and ancient temple scene, and the charging stand picks up that weathered stone look. It's a different approach, and I rather like it. There's something about the Pro 3's shape, too, that reminds me of the old PS2 DualShock. It's lighter and a little more plasticky than the Ultimate 3, but still comfortable to hold, with a nice tactile feel to the buttons.

Sources indicate that this is the one I'd look at if I were playing on Switch 2, especially if you want to revisit the Tomb Raider: Definitive Survivor Trilogy on Nintendo's console. It's a good-looking pad; the Lost Valley artwork is lovely, and the included stand gives it personality when you're not playing. It's also a capable modern controller, with TMR sticks and Hall-effect triggers, so you don't feel like you're buying it purely for the artwork.

It has been revealed that but I keep glancing back at the Ultimate 3. The Pro 3 is perfectly good and arguably has a stronger connection to the original 1996 game, but it doesn't quite have the same sense of occasion. Its unboxing is much more straightforward, and I never thought I'd say this, but I'd happily pay the extra for the Ultimate 3 packaging. The fact that the controller feels better made is a bonus.

I've always thought of collectable gaming hardware as something that looks nice in a display cabinet but doesn't necessarily earn its place in everyday use, and I think that's what has surprised me most about these two pads. The Ultimate 3 has made me reconsider my somewhat cynical approach to collectable controllers, as it’s a gamepad I actually want to use, but I also like having it on my desk, and the whole thing was designed with that in mind.

Sources indicate that switch 2 players shouldn't feel left out. The Pro 3 is a lovely alternative, and if you're particularly fond of the original Tomb Raider, there's a lot to like about its Lost Valley design. But if you're after the full treasure-hunter experience, the Ultimate 3 is the one that has me reaching for my wallet. And that's something I really didn't expect to say about a controller.

Visit the 8Bitdo Tomb Raider website for more info.

Starvation Mode: How Caloric Restriction Affects Your Body

📅 31 Aug 2024 | ⏱️ 3 min read (646 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cutting back on calories but not losing weight?
  • Recent findings suggest that everyone from your personal trainer to your grandma may have warned you about this metabolic frenemy that keeps your body holding onto weight.
  • The concept of starvation mode is that when you restrict calories, your body has a “hold it right there” response.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cutting back on calories but not losing weight? You might wonder if you’ve gotten stuck in the twilight zone of so-called “starvation mode.”.

Recent findings suggest that everyone from your personal trainer to your grandma may have warned you about this metabolic frenemy that keeps your body holding onto weight. But is starvation mode really a thing — or just an urban legend?

The concept of starvation mode is that when you restrict calories, your body has a “hold it right there” response. To prevent you from losing weight rapidly, your metabolism slows, conserving energy by reducing the calories it burns.

According to recent reports, research highlights starvation mode — formally called adaptive thermogenesis or metabolic adaptation — is a legit phenomenon. It’s well documented that sometimes, the more weight you lose (and the more rapidly you do so), the more your body resists the process.

Evolutionarily speaking, this may be a holdover from when humans faced food scarcity and needed a mechanism for self-preservation. But in today’s world, starvation mode can be a frustrating roadblock to weight loss.

What does this metabolic hiccup look like? These symptoms may indicate that starvation mode is becoming a problem for your health:.

It has been revealed that starvation mode isn’t the same thing as actual starving. In today’s modern food environment, true starvation is rare. If you’re eating regularly, you won’t experience life-threatening starvation.

Industry observers note that however, your body might exhibit some of the same early signs as real starvation. These include the symptoms listed above.

Most commonly, though, starvation mode involves stalled weight loss. You may have hit the wall of adaptive thermogenesis when restricting calories and increasing physical activity without losing weight.

Getting into starvation mode can take just a few days, especially if those days involve severe calorie restriction.

So what counts as severe calorie restriction? Many experts advise not going below 1,200 calories per day for women and 1,500 calories per day for men unless supervised by a doctor. Anything below these numbers could land you in starvation mode faster.

Fortunately, getting your body out of starvation mode isn’t complicated.

According to recent reports, first, there’s the obvious solution: Eat a few more calories. But we don’t mean just any calories. By adding a few more nutrient-dense foods (especially those with fiber and protein), you may find weight loss becomes easier, not harder. Both of these nutrients have links to weight loss — so they might help you get out of starvation mode without gaining weight.

If you’re feeling extremely depleted, you might take a temporary break from a weight loss diet to replenish your nutrient stores.

Choosing the proper exercise could also bump you out of starvation mode. Resistance exercises like weightlifting, yoga, push-ups, squats, and others build muscle, which increases your metabolic rate.

According to a 2014 study, people who participated in a 9-month resistance exercise program increased their resting metabolic rate — aka how many calories they burned at rest — by an average of 5%.

Sources indicate that weight loss is a balancing act. It’s normal to experience physical and emotional ups and downs.

In a recent development, that said, it’s time to see a doctor if you’re noticing symptoms like extreme fatigue or lethargy, constipation that lasts more than a few days, sensitivity to cold, or unusual mood changes. Your healthcare team can help you hit the sweet spot of weight loss without lingering in starvation mode.

According to recent reports, despite its name, being in starvation mode doesn’t mean you’ll starve. Instead, it’s a state in which your body has adapted to your weight loss efforts, giving you pushback on how many calories it burns. With strategies like tweaking your calorie intake and adding strength training, you can get out of this mode and back on the path to sustained weight loss.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

One of the highest-value redemptions in travel rewards.

Picture this: you're settling into a lie-flat business class seat somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of something cold in hand, knowing that in 48 hours you'll be waking up in Istanbul — and then, a few days later, continuing onward to Bangkok. Two bucket-list cities. One award booking. One points balance. This is what the Aeroplan stopover sweet spot feels like in practice. It's not a trick or a loophole — it's a deliberately designed feature of Air Canada's Aeroplan program that the vast majority of travelers simply don't know exists. And that gap between awareness and reality is exactly where the ChooseFI community finds its edge. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A business class itinerary from North America to Istanbul with a continuing flight onward to Bangkok — two long-haul segments, lie-flat seats, Star Alliance lounges at every connection — would cost somewhere between **$6,000 and $15,000 in cash**. That's a realistic retail range depending on season and how far out you book. Most people never consider it a possibility for a family vacation or a milestone trip because the sticker price puts it in a different universe. With Aeroplan, you're booking that same itinerary — the same seats, the same lounges, the same Turkish Airlines or Thai Airways product — for **75,000 Aeroplan points**. At the low end of the cash price range, that's already **8 cents per point**. At the high end, you're extracting **20 cents per point** from a currency that most people earned by putting groceries on a credit card. The pricing inefficiency here is structural. Aeroplan's partner award chart prices long-haul business class at a fixed rate regardless of cash fare fluctuations. When business class prices spike — around holidays, during peak travel seasons, during major events — your points cost stays exactly the same. You're insulated from the market. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: you've already paid for the trip in points, slowly accumulated through everyday spending, and now you're simply redeeming the stored value. The stopover itself is nearly free. Aeroplan charges just 5,000 extra miles to add a stopover city to a one-way award. That means your Istanbul layover becomes a multi-day stay — at zero additional points cost beyond that small add-on — and you haven't booked a second award at all. One booking. Two destinations. That's the entire premise, and once you see it, you can't unsee it.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you understand it, but it requires knowing three things that most travelers don't: how Aeroplan's routing rules work, what a stopover actually is in the context of an award ticket, and why Star Alliance's global network makes this scalable to almost any destination pair you can imagine.

When Aeroplan relaunched its loyalty program in 2020, it did something remarkable: it eliminated fuel surcharges entirely and published a partner award chart with fixed pricing for flights on Star Alliance carriers. This is critical. When you book Turkish Airlines business class through Aeroplan, you pay the Aeroplan fixed chart rate — not what Turkish Airlines would charge in its own currency or miles program, and not the inflated cash price. That fixed chart is the engine of this redemption.

For long-haul international business class, Aeroplan's chart prices routing through multiple regions based on your origin and destination — not every intermediate stop. This is the aha moment. Aeroplan determines your award price based on where your journey starts and where it ends, and then allows you to add a stopover in between for just 5,000 additional miles. The stopover city is priced as a pass-through for the purpose of calculating your award zone, not as a second trip.

On a one-way Aeroplan award, you're permitted to add a free stopover — meaning you can stay in an intermediate city for any length of time before continuing to your final destination. That 5,000-mile add-on is essentially the cost of a full additional destination. Compare that to booking a second one-way award from Istanbul to Bangkok, which would cost you another 40,000–55,000 Aeroplan points in business class. The math is decisive.

Recent findings suggest that the routing must be geographically sensible — you can't fly backwards across the globe — but Aeroplan's allowance for multi-segment itineraries through Star Alliance hubs gives you enormous flexibility. Istanbul (IST) is a Turkish Airlines hub. Bangkok (BKK) is served by Thai Airways and several Star Alliance carriers. Both are Star Alliance partners. Both are bookable through Aeroplan at fixed chart rates with no fuel surcharges.

Industry observers note that the best part for the ChooseFI community is how accessible the underlying points are. Aeroplan accepts transfers from four major programs:.

It has been revealed that chase's instant transfer speed is particularly valuable here. When you find business class availability — which can disappear quickly — you want to move points immediately. Having Chase Ultimate Rewards as your primary earning currency means you can search, find space, and transfer points before the availability window closes. The 1:1 ratio across all four programs means no conversion math — every point you earn translates directly to one Aeroplan mile.

Booking an Aeroplan stopover award in business class is genuinely one of the more complex redemptions in the travel rewards world, but it becomes manageable when you break it into distinct phases. Here's exactly how to do it.

Start by deciding on your two destinations. Aeroplan stopovers work best when your intermediate city is a major Star Alliance hub that lies geographically between your origin and final destination. Classic combinations include North America to Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub) continuing to Southeast Asia, or North America to a European hub continuing to the Middle East or East Africa. Your stopover city should be somewhere you genuinely want to spend 2–5 days — this is a real trip, not just a layover.

This is the most important and most time-consuming step. You need to find saver-level business class availability on both segments independently before you book.

Once you've confirmed availability on both segments, go to aeroplan.com and use the multi-city search function. Enter your full itinerary — origin, stopover city with your intended layover dates, and final destination.

Once you've confirmed the award is bookable and are ready to complete the reservation:.

Recent findings suggest that complete your booking on aeroplan.com or with a phone agent, confirm the stopover is properly reflected in your itinerary, and save every confirmation email. Verify your seats on each carrier's website immediately after booking.

According to recent reports, A stopover is an intentional break in your journey lasting more than 24 hours at a connecting city. Most airlines treat stopovers as separate tickets, charging full price for each segment. Aeroplan is one of the few programs that allows a free stopover on round-trip awards, letting you explore a connecting city for days before continuing to your final destination. This is fundamentally different from a layover, which is a brief connection of a few hours at an airport. The stopover must be in a city served by a Star Alliance carrier on your routing, and the key is that Aeroplan prices the entire itinerary as one award, not two.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Studio operations software Programa has redesigned its programme to rethink how interior design studios operate, giving practices more flexibility and freeing up their time.

According to Programa, beautiful interiors are built on “hundreds of decisions”, which take long periods of time to decide upon and patch across multiple spreadsheets.

Each decision brings specification details, quantities, pricing and revisions that studios must keep updated as a project develops.

These include minute, precise details such as dimensions, materials, finishes, technical requirements, and component quantities.

Programa‘s redesigned programme keeps a record of each item used in an interior project, from furniture and lighting to hardware and finishes, and optimises their organisation based on how the project runs.

The firm explained that increased AI use is making convincing images “easier to generate than ever”, yet clients often run into logistical challenges when using this alone.

For example, the AI model doesn’t take into account whether a wardrobe or sofa fits through the door, suits the needs of the people living there, or whether the overall design takes full advantage of a space’s natural light.

With Programa, the designer can smoothly make these judgements using the software’s organisation of specifications, cost, quantities and overall project coordination.

The company explained that if a designer updates a product’s shared specification once, the change appears in the Programa schedules that include it, while quantities can be individually allocated by room.

For Austin Carrier of Californian design studio, Hommeboys Interiors, this is particularly helpful.

“We use schedules for everything from lighting and hardware to plumbing fixtures and furniture, indoor and outdoor,” Carrier explained.

“For furniture, we can break down every room, then the pieces within that room, and give clients several options to reject or accept,” he added.

In a recent development, as a result, the software aims to cut the “gruelling amount of work” updating schedules, preparing presentations, and communicating with suppliers. It also reduces repeated data entry, freeing up time.

The platform is defined as an “alternative to spreadsheets”, which often have to be made from scratch and reformatted for different presentations.

Recent findings suggest that “The issue with the spreadsheet is that it’s like a blank cell,” added Los Angeles-based designer Paul Chan. “You can put anything in there – it doesn’t carry from one project to another.”.

“With Programa, I can take a format from one project and move it into the next,” Chan continued. “There’s consistency between each project.”.

Specifically, the Programa Schedule function details the items’ code, supplier, finish, dimensions, quantity and price.

It offers a streamlined place to reference drawings, get client approval and work with contractors to meet on-site deadlines.

The organization explained that one of its platform’s main benefits is that it can be used from early product decision-making through to final delivery.

Here, the studio manages the specification and controls what is shared, whereas the clients review selections and provide approvals. Collaborators also receive the information relevant to their work.

“Once we get all of the information in there, we can send it out in one email to all of our vendors, and then they are able to get us pricing back very easily,” added Tana Nesbitt-Hayes of Studio 8 Architect.

It has been revealed that “If we’re exceeding our budget in one area, we can tailor it back. It’s always up-to-date.”.

“We share our Programa Schedules with the millworkers and the engineers,” she added. “They can see the refrigerator we’re going to put in, and they can make the panels to fit.”.

Programa offers a free trial for all studios. To learn more, visit its website.

Sources indicate that this is inflammation of the nasal vestibule, the area just inside your nostrils, often caused by bacterial infections. It can lead to painful, red bumps sensitive to the touch. Common triggers include frequent nose-picking, blowing too hard, or even plucking nose hairs.

According to recent reports, when you pluck or trim nose hairs, the hair can sometimes grow back into the skin instead of out, causing an ingrown hair. If this becomes infected, it can result in a painful bump inside the nose.

A bump can also form inside the nose due to trauma, such as a blow to the nose, or even from something as simple as aggressive nose-picking. The trauma can cause the tissue to swell or become bruised. In some cases, a hard bump may form as the tissue heals.

Fluid-filled sacs that can form in your nose, usually harmless but sometimes uncomfortable.

A hard bump inside the nose might be due to problems with the cartilage, such as a deviated septum or cartilage overgrowth.

Small, benign bumps that may appear on or in the nose are often mistaken for pimples but are fibrous tissue growths.

Breaking: Seaweed earplug among grant-winning Design Museum prototypes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A single-use earplug crafted from seaweed, two plant-based insulation materials and a homegrown timber kit-of-parts for low-rise buildings are among the projects that have been awarded Design Museum grants.
  • UK-based studios Searo Labs, WeCanMake, Local Works Studio and SY Ecofit have been granted a share of £280,000 from the Design Museum for their “cutting-edge” environmental prototypes.
  • Described as the “world’s first seaweed-based single-use earplug”, SearoSoft by Cambridge-based Searo Labs is a fully biodegradable and renewable alternative to single-use earplugs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A single-use earplug crafted from seaweed, two plant-based insulation materials and a homegrown timber kit-of-parts for low-rise buildings are among the projects that have been awarded Design Museum grants.

UK-based studios Searo Labs, WeCanMake, Local Works Studio and SY Ecofit have been granted a share of £280,000 from the Design Museum for their “cutting-edge” environmental prototypes.

Described as the “world’s first seaweed-based single-use earplug”, SearoSoft by Cambridge-based Searo Labs is a fully biodegradable and renewable alternative to single-use earplugs.

According to SearoSoft, the soft, mouldable earplugs are made without microplastics or chemicals and designed to hydrate the ear canal, unlike plastic-based products, which can be drying.

Once discarded, they are biodegradable in water or soil after 30 days. As seaweed is a regenerative crop, SearoSoft explained that there is no need for land, freshwater or fertilisers, making the process simple and more sustainable.

It has been revealed that among the other prototypes is a building material project by Sussex-based Local Works Studio. The initiative, named Ferment, will repurpose agricultural waste into an insulating material fit for retrofitting buildings.

Local Works Studio aims to develop an accessible product for farms via what it calls a “harvest-to-house system”, where farmers can produce the insulation themselves using their existing infrastructure, skills and machinery.

Bristol-based studio WeCanMake’s winning prototype, Neighbourhood Factory Futures, is a homegrown timber kit-of-parts system designed to be used for constructing low-rise apartment buildings.

With the Design Museum’s grant, the studio plans to create a neighbourhood factory model, allowing local communities to build and maintain their own homes.

WeCanMake explained it created the system as part of a wider movement aiming to make the UK a “nation of growers, producers and makers” while using reusable materials that store, rather than emit, carbon.

Prototyping PhytoFloc by social enterprise SY Ecofit in collaboration with Phyona and Studio Bio is a zero-waste project that, similarly to Local Works Studio, aims to develop plant-based insulation for building construction.

The project uses biowaste created as a byproduct of phytomining, where former industrial land is rejuvenated by plants that extract pollutants from the soil.

The project intends to recognise the value of post-industrial soils while creating a locally made, low-carbon material.

According to recent reports, the grants are part of the Design Museum’s Future Observatory program, which is run in partnership with the Arts and Humanities Research Council. The winning projects were amongst 140 prototypes that were submitted to the scheme.

The museum explained that at a time when supply chains are under pressure, the Future Observatory aims to support designers’ practical research to drive the green transition.

“The climate crisis demands rapid change, and we believe that design is critically important if we are to meet that challenge,” remarked Design Museum director Tim Marlow.

“The presence of Future Observatory allows us an extraordinary opportunity to get involved with practitioners and problem-solvers and have a direct impact on the development of new technologies at the frontier of current design thinking.”.

The four projects will be funded from November 2026 until July 2027. Afterwards, the prototypes will be tested and begin the commercialisation process.

#22490. Latest Update: Are GLP-1 Drugs Quietly Changing Our Sex Lives?

📅 10 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2090 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Are GLP-1 Drugs Quietly Changing Our Sex Lives?

📅 10 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2090 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that by now you’ve probably heard about GLP-1s, sold under brand names such as Ozempic and Wegovy.
  • At present roughly one in five Americans reports taking or having taken a GLP-1, according to a recent poll.
  • In a review published in Obesity Pillars in March 2026, for example, researchers propose that GLP-1s may influence desire by impacting brain chemistry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that by now you’ve probably heard about GLP-1s, sold under brand names such as Ozempic and Wegovy. This class of medications mimics naturally occurring hormones involved in appetite control and blood sugar regulation to treat type 2 diabetes and aid weight-loss efforts. It should be no surprise, then, that conversations around these popular drugs have largely centered on the scale. However, some scientists are starting to look more closely into how they may impact something perhaps even more personal: our sex lives.

At present roughly one in five Americans reports taking or having taken a GLP-1, according to a recent poll. As the number of people using these medications has soared, so have anecdotal reports about how they’re impacting consumers’ day-to-day—and yes, this includes things like pleasure and sex drive. Though there hasn’t been a ton of research into the relationship between sexual health and GLP-1s yet, more scientists are starting to investigate potential impacts.

In a review published in Obesity Pillars in March 2026, for example, researchers propose that GLP-1s may influence desire by impacting brain chemistry. But how exactly might these drugs impact sex drive? And is there a way to remain engaged in your sex life while on a GLP-1? We tapped experts to find out.

To understand how GLP-1s might influence libido, it helps to walk through how they work more broadly.

According to recent reports, some options, like Wegovy and Ozempic, contain semaglutide, which is a synthetic version of a naturally occurring hormone, glucagon-like peptide-1, or GLP-1. Semaglutide binds to GLP-1 receptors throughout the brain and body, helping regulate appetite, blood sugar, and feelings of satiety, James Simon, MD, an ob-gyn and reproductive endocrinologist and one of the researchers behind the Obesity Pillars study, tells SELF.

Other options, like Zepbound and Mounjaro, contain a different active ingredient called tirzepatide, which mimics both GLP-1 and a related hormone, and thus impacts the body in similar ways to semaglutide.

On top of reporting reduced appetite and increased satiety, a number of patients have also found that these weight-loss medications quiet what they call “food noise.” But as it turns out, the same parts of the brain that control appetite are also responsible for other reward-seeking behaviors, according to Dr. Simon. He indicates this could help explain why taking GLP-1s may have the auxiliary impact of decreasing appetite for another pleasurable activity: sex.

On top of that, early research suggests that GLP-1s may affect certain serotonin receptors, including one called 5-HT2C. This is thought to be a key player in the sexual side effects often experienced by those taking selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as reduced libido and delayed orgasm.

According to recent reports, “We know that, while SSRIs are fantastic options for anxiety and depression, they can have a significant impact on sexual desire and orgasmic function in both men and women,” claims Dr. Simon. “It makes sense that other medications that also impact serotonin pathways might have similar impacts on sexual desire in some individuals.”.

Sexual function isn’t just about hormones and brain chemistry. It also depends on the pelvic floor, a group of muscles that support the bladder and bowel, among other organs, and play an active role in arousal and orgasm, explains pelvic-health physical therapist Iris Xu, PT, DPT, of Fusion Wellness & Femina Physical Therapy.

“During arousal the pelvic-floor muscles increase blood flow to the genitals,” Dr. Xu claims. During penetration the muscles lengthen and relax to allow for comfortable insertion and boost sensation. And during orgasm they contract rhythmically, creating the pulsing feeling associated with climax, she says.

In general, weight loss—from GLP-1s or other methods—can improve pelvic-floor function because reduced abdominal pressure means the muscles don’t have to work as hard to support the pelvic organs, Dr. Xu indicates. A 2024 study published in Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics found that women carrying more fat, particularly in the pelvic area, had weaker pelvic floor muscles than those with less.

Recent findings suggest that but GLP-1s don’t just encourage fat loss. Because these medications can lead to relatively rapid weight loss, preserving lean muscle mass can be challenging—especially without adequate protein intake or resistance training, says Dr. Xu. “[GLP-1s] can also cause loss of lean body mass and strength, especially when used in isolation without exercise or diet modifications,” she adds. In extreme cases this can lead to a condition called sarcopenia, which some studies have linked to reduced pelvic floor function. (FWIW, muscle loss can occur no matter how you lose weight. But by accelerating the weight-loss process, GLP-1s may speed up muscle loss as well.).

At the time of writing, research specifically examining GLP-1 medications and pelvic-floor outcomes remains limited. There is also little data on these drugs’ impact on muscle loss. But the research we do have points to this being a likely outcome, and Dr. Xu states losing too much lean mass may weaken pelvic floor support. This, in turn, can affect arousal, orgasm intensity, or overall sexual function.

As mentioned earlier, part of the notoriety of these medications is the speed at which many patients lose weight. Research has shown that, on average, people who are overweight or living with obesity can lose anywhere from roughly 10% to 20% of their total body weight on a GLP-1, depending on factors like which drug they use, what dose they take, and how long they continue treatment.

However, despite cultural messages to the contrary, weight loss does not automatically translate to increased body confidence and desire, Joy Berkheimer, PhD, LMFT, a sex and relationship therapist, tells SELF.

Recent findings suggest that “Particularly if you have a long history of having your body policed against external beauty standards—as most women and people assigned female at birth do—the rapidity of the physical changes can lead you to feel unfamiliar in your body,” she states. Sexual desire and pleasure are often closely tied to embodiment, so a lack of embodiment can impact intimacy, she says.

It’s not all bad news; for some people the broader health changes associated with these drugs may actually improve aspects of sexual well-being. People go on GLP-1s for help with a variety of health conditions, such as obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), to name just a few. Addressing these sorts of underlying complications may benefit sexual health.

That means even if the medications dial down some of the brain signals tied to desire, other changes happening in the body (e.g., improved energy, hormone balance, and physical comfort) may help support a healthier sex life, Dr. Simon tells SELF.

“Fat cells are highly inflammatory and impede our well-being far beyond their impact on our weight, leading to things such as joint pain and muscle fatigue,” he states. Feeling weak and achy can reduce interest in any physical activity—sex included!—as well as decrease pleasure during them. But as fat mass decreases and inflammation drops, people may feel more comfortable, energetic, and ultimately sexier. Additionally, as body composition improves, hormone levels may shift in ways that boost sexual desire and function, particularly in those with dysfunction, Dr. Simon says. (Body fat contains enzymes that can convert testosterone into estrogen. When levels of these hormones are unbalanced, it can impact sexual health.).

Sources indicate that GLP-1 medications have also been shown to improve markers associated with vascular health, including blood pressure. Healthy blood flow is essential to arousal in people of all genders, claims Dr. Simon. For those with vaginas it supports clitoral engorgement, lubrication, and vaginal expansion.

Finally, as metabolic health improves some people will see an increase in their energy levels and feel more comfortable in their bodies, indicates board-certified bariatric surgeon and obesity medicine specialist Betsy Dovec, MD, FACS, DBOM. For some—particularly those navigating postpartum body changes or the menopause transition—that renewed energy and groundedness can translate into increased confidence and desire, she says.

Taken altogether these physiological shifts can enhance sexual function for some people, even as the medications potentially continue to lower the volume on certain reward pathways.

In a recent development, of course, our sex lives aren’t driven by biology alone. They are mediated by culture and society, the relationships we’re in, our sense of self and self-confidence, and more. The broader life changes that can accompany weight loss may shift libido north or south.

Industry observers note that in a society that often equates thinness with desirability, people who don’t fall into the narrow confines of “thin” may feel undesirable, unsexy, or even undeserving of pleasure. For some individuals changes in body composition toward that supposed ideal may lead to increased confidence.

In a recent development, A 2025 survey from the Kinsey Institute and DatingAdvice.com found that 59% of GLP-1 agonist owners noted the medication had an impact on their dating life, with a number saying it boosted their confidence. Justin Lehmiller, PhD, a social psychologist, research fellow at the Kinsey Institute, and host of the Sex and Psychology podcast, tells SELF that confidence can have huge impacts on our sexual satisfaction.

“Feeling confident makes it easier to surrender to pleasure and facilitates communicating about our sexual needs and desires, which helps to ensure that we’re getting more of what we want in bed,” he says. “By contrast, when we aren’t feeling confident, it’s easy to get stuck in our heads during intimacy and start worrying about things like how we look.”.

For those who are single, increased self-confidence may inspire someone who previously didn’t use dating apps or go out to bars because of body image hang-ups to start putting themselves in situations where connection feels more possible, Dr. Simon notes. Meanwhile, in long-term relationships that confidence could translate into greater willingness to initiate sex or say yes to a partner’s advances, he adds. It may also mean someone feels more comfortable experimenting with positions they once shied away from—potentially even discovering ones that bring them more pleasure.

Industry observers note that in these cases the reward pathways are still muted. However, because other things that shape sexual desire and enjoyment (like confidence) have increased, patients on these drugs may be experiencing better and/or more sex overall.

According to recent reports, “Changes in libido are among the most common concerns people bring into sex therapy,” Dr. Berkheimer states. “But often they are a completely normal response to life transitions or physiological shifts, rather than a sign that something is wrong.”.

According to recent reports, desire isn’t static, she explains. Rather, it fluctuates across the lifespan in response to factors like stress, sleep quality, exercise routine, medication, illness, hormones, relationship dynamics, and more. That means any shifts you notice after starting a GLP-1 medication aren’t necessarily a sign that something is off—your body might just need time to adjust, Dr. Berkheimer indicates. Still, if the change feels distressing or different enough to affect your well-being or relationships, it’s worth bringing up with your doctor.

Sexual health, Dr. Dovec states, isn’t a frivolous concern. “Pleasure matters. Intimacy matters. Feeling sexy matters. These are at the core of quality of life,” she says. Shifts in sexual desire and function can offer useful information about what’s happening in your body more broadly. So if sexual changes happen, talk to your provider. As frustrating or unwelcome as these shifts can be, they’re often temporary or solvable with a provider’s help, according to Dr. Dovec.

Sometimes the solution is as simple as adjusting GLP-1 dosage or timing; other times a clinician may suggest lifestyle changes, like adjusting your diet or exercise routine, or additional treatments that support hormone balance.

Not sure how to start the conversation? Dr. Dovec suggests keeping it simple: “You can just say, ‘Something feels different,’ or ‘I don’t feel like myself sexually.’ You’re not going to shock or embarrass your doctor.”.

If you find yourself missing pleasure during this season of libidinal lull, Dr. Berkheimer encourages approaching your body with curiosity rather than pressure and expanding intimacy beyond intercourse. “That can look like slowing down and focusing on sensation instead of performance, exploring non-goal-oriented touch like massage or extended skin-to-skin contact, [or experimenting with] sex toys or pleasure aids,” she tells SELF.

Sources indicate that working with a body-neutral or Health at Every Size (HAES) sex therapist can also help you navigate medication effects, physical changes, identity, cultural conditioning, and more so you can erect an updated pleasure practice that honors the body you’re in now, Dr. Berkheimer adds.

  • According to recent reports, when I moved to Italy in 2024, one of the first things I noticed was the very particular way Italian nonne, or grandmas, live.
  • According to recent reports, I was then delighted—and unsurprised—when I came across a latest wellness trend making the rounds on social media.
  • Sources indicate that there’s certainly a lot to learn from Italian grandmothers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when I moved to Italy in 2024, one of the first things I noticed was the very particular way Italian nonne, or grandmas, live. They walk everywhere, frequently across the city, without any assistance. Many of them are dressed to the nines, but they also don’t try to hide their age.

According to recent reports, I was then delighted—and unsurprised—when I came across a latest wellness trend making the rounds on social media. “Nonnamaxxing” is the idea that anyone can maximize their life if they just embrace the habits of Italian grandmas. It happens to be sensible guidance.

Sources indicate that there’s certainly a lot to learn from Italian grandmothers. Italy leads the European Union in life expectancy, and it’s a country where the number of centenarians is growing. A cluster of villages in Sardinia is one of the world’s five Blue Zones. Online guidance includes ditching social media, eating homemade everything, wearing cotton nightgowns, and welcoming unhurried lunches with friends. Some of these suggestions line up with how I’ve seen Italian grandmas live. But as a health and science journalist, I’ve noticed there’s more to it than what looks good on Instagram or TikTok. In fact, Licia Fertz, a 96-year-old Italian nonna based in Viterbo, Italy, tells SELF, quite the opposite is true.

“I put on my makeup and dress in cheerful colors, even if I’m not leaving the house, because presenting yourself well is an act of self-love,” Fertz says.

Industry observers note that it seems that Italian nonne are the health gurus we all need. Read on to learn their secrets to a happier, healthier, and longer life.

According to recent reports, I rarely see Italian nonne who don’t look their age. In fact, it’s one of the first things I noticed when I moved here. At the pools and beaches, it doesn’t matter how old they are; women, nonne included, frequently wear bikinis. Honestly, it’s refreshing and emphasizes a cultural mindset that aging is a natural part of life.

Fertz tells SELF that this mindset is key to her living a long and healthy life. “Never think of yourself as old,” indicates Fertz. “You are born young.”.

It turns out that as you age, having a more positive attitude about getting older could help you live longer too. A recent study found an association between how women view aging and the actual pace at which they age.

In a recent development, sonja Lyubomirsky, a distinguished professor of psychology at the University of California, Riverside, and author of How To Feel Loved, tells SELF that a mindset is like putting on a pair of glasses or a coat. “It certainly matters very much what our mindset is when we think about aging,” Lyubomirsky indicates. “Is it a gift? Is it about wisdom, maturity, and the richness of life, or is it about deterioration and loss?” Both can be true, she says. “But you can choose.”.

At school pick-up for my daughter, I don’t only see other parents. I also see Italian nonne. That’s because Italian grandmas are very involved in their grandkids’ lives and take an active role in caregiving. In fact, for better or worse, the Italian economy is supported by the unpaid labor of Italian grandmothers—and this is well-known and discussed in local mom groups.

According to recent reports, research demonstrates that caregiving later in life may lead to better aging and act as a buffer against cognitive decline. One recent study found that grandparents who provided childcare—ranging from caring for sick grandkids, helping with homework, or driving them to school—scored higher on memory and verbal fluency tests compared with those who didn’t help with childcare.

“I live with my grandson,” Fertz tells SELF. “I’m a great-grandmother, and every day spent with my great-granddaughter is a gift that never ceases to amaze me.”.

Sources indicate that even if you’re not a grandparent, helping others can yield similar health benefits. According to research published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine, people who volunteered more than 100 hours a year—versus those who volunteered zero hours a year—had a reduced risk of mortality, more optimism, and purpose in their lives.

Recent findings suggest that italian cities and villages are highly walkable, meaning walking isn’t something people do for exercise; it’s just a way of life. Even if someone has a car, sometimes a destination is only reachable by foot because Italy’s infamously narrow streets. Gas is also more expensive in Italy. While this might be inconvenient for some, a walking-first lifestyle happens to be associated with longevity.

Sources indicate that “Walking is the most fundamental form of human physical activity and many, many hundreds of studies confirm that walking helps people age slower and better,” Daniel Lieberman, a professor of Human Evolutionary Biology at Harvard University, tells SELF. “Walking helps you age well.”.

It has been revealed that paola Mariotti, a pediatrician and nonna based in Florence, Italy, tells SELF that walking is very important to her, and was very important to her own grandparents, who didn’t have a car and walked everywhere. Today, as a more modern nonna, Mariotti focuses on walking at least 5,000 steps a day—which she tracks on her phone—but strives to get 10,000 steps or more, if possible, each day.

Much of America isn’t walkable, but a 2025 study published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine found that even 15 minutes of fast walking a day can reduce premature death.

It has been revealed that at cafés in Italy, I’m always struck by how Italian nonne drink un caffè. Usually, she is just enjoying her coffee and watching people walk by, rather than scrolling on her phone or sending emails on her laptop. Some might call this the dolce far niente, which means the sweetness of doing nothing. While it’s true that these moments of pause and presence are more common in Italy, there’s something deeper to them. They reflect how, as a culture, Italians are content to live more mindfully. They appreciate quality over quantity and don’t feel the need to constantly multitask for the sake of being productive.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, Jonathan Alpert, a psychotherapist in Latest York, tells SELF that he thinks nonnamaxxing has less to do with actual Italian grandmothers and more about Gen Z’s desire to escape hustle culture. “The appeal here is the fantasy of a life that feels grounded, warm, and unhurried,” Alpert says. “A lot of younger people are burned out by the pressure to constantly optimize themselves, be productive, and turn their lives into content.”.

While in the moment, multitasking can feel like you’re being more efficient, researchers say that it actually does the opposite and can lead to increased stress levels.

The antidote to hustle culture is a mindful one. This can be as simple as just enjoying a coffee without much else, as it’s been found that people who stay in the present moment age better and with more resilience.

Industry observers note that in Italy, there’s an emphasis on eating what’s in season. In fact, my local market provides customers with a chart that identifies exactly what fruits and vegetables are in season each month. This lifestyle isn’t exactly optional—produce that’s out-of-season is harder to come by. Antonino De Lorenzo, professor emeritus of human nutrition at the University of Rome Tor Vergata, tells SELF that the value isn’t in the variety of food, but in what’s gained when you choose seasonal produce, which is food that is less likely to have preservatives and industrial products.

It has been revealed that “Freshness, variety, ripeness, and preparation methods can all exert a significant influence on a food’s nutritional profile,” De Lorenzo claims. “A high-quality diet, maintained over time, promotes healthier aging, characterized by better preservation of physical, mental, and cognitive functions, as well as reduced exposure to major chronic diseases.”.

Indeed, the Mediterranean diet, which focuses on olive oil, vegetables, fruits, whole grains and legumes—all popular in Italy—has been linked to longevity. As researchers tend to emphasize, the Mediterranean diet isn’t a fad diet. It’s a way of life.

Italian grandmas are stereotypically known for being connected to their communities and neighbors—maybe even a bit too much, in the sense that it can veer into nosiness. Viral videos on social media have joked that Italian nonne are Italy’s security systems.

According to recent reports, “The most vital thing for living a long and happy life? Don’t isolate yourself,” Fertz notes. “Always stay in touch with people, travel, plan outings, and get out of the house.”.

According to recent reports, according to a study in The American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry, having a sense of purpose can help preserve cognitive function as you age. A separate study found that people with a higher sense of purpose had a reduced risk for depression and loneliness. Whether that is being in-the-know in your community, or finding a hobby to keep you busy, the key is to feel connected and busy.

Because boredom, Fertz says, is “the one thing that truly makes you old.”.

Before you double-over during your next marathon, here’s what to know.

That fateful stab in your side is most likely to happen during exercise where your upper bod states tight and upright for an extended period, such as when you run, jog, bike, hike, play soccer, etc.

It has been revealed that this common prob has been around for ages — the first historical mention is from ancient Roman philosopher Pliny the Elder. Yet, scientists still haven’t reached a consensus on its exact cause. We know that it affects up to 70% of runners each year.

It’s also more likely to occur on the right side.

A stiff spine or poor posture (according to older research from 2010) could contribute to side stitches – but TBH, the pros don’t know for sure.

Sources indicate that according to a 2022 review, researchers also think a side stitch might be caused by your right foot hitting the ground while you breathe out, irritating a phrenic nerve. Researchers think this, in turn, may bother the lining of your abdomen (particularly on the lower right side). Since most people are right-foot dominant, this is one possible explanation.

Experts also theorize that it could be triggered by the boost of blood flow around the diaphragm when running.

Furthermore, fueling up before a big race is excellent — but eating or drinking large quantities right before running may boost your risk of getting a side stitch, anecdotal reports suggest.

Images courtesy of Waugh Thistleton Architects.

UK studio Waugh Thistleton Architects is set to transform the Edwardian Westbrook Pavilion in Margate, UK, into an arts centre for British artist Tracey Emin with a cafe, public sauna and changing rooms.

“The project will bring a much-loved seafront building back into use, combining its original purpose with newly introduced spaces for art, culture and the local community,” said Waugh Thistleton Architects.

The studio recently won planning permission from the local council to convert the abandoned building, which Emin purchased in 2023, into a facility run by the Tracey Emin Foundation.

The project aims to return the building to its former use as a changing room for swimmers and as a tea room, when it originally opened in 1914.

“Originally opened in 1914, the building provided public changing facilities for sea-bathing and a tea room,” said the studio.

“Following storm damage in the Great North Sea Storm of 1953, subsequent alterations detracted from its original Edwardian character,” it continued.

“The renovated pavilion will accommodate artist studios, an art gallery, clubroom, cafe, sea-bathing changing facilities, a latest sauna and refurbished public toilets, restoring its original role as a place for bathing and socialising by the sea.”.

Along with making the pavilion a building used by the public again, the studio aims to return the building’s core to its Edwardian look by removing later additions. It will also add glazed facades to the wings on either side of the central pavilion.

The building will be topped by a rooftop terrace, while a public toilet on the site will be renovated.

“The design draws on the proportions and character of the original building, removing later additions and reinstating lost features such as the historic belvederes which top the central tower structures,” said the studio.

“The beachfront facade will see a latest glazing system and colonnade to each of the building’s wings, with a new sheltered archway forming a new seating terrace at the building’s heart,” it continued.

“The design seeks to reference the original architecture while providing contemporary needs of a public building. Where original features are references, these are distinguishable architecturally.”.

It has been revealed that emin is one of the UK’s best-known living artists. We recently produced a video of a landmark exhibition of her work at Tate Modern.

Recent projects by Waugh Thistleton Architects include plans for the “tallest mass timber office building in the US”.

Industry News: 6 Supplements Doctors Actually Take

📅 10 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1496 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These days, it seems like everyone is taking a supplement—to look better, think better, sleep better, relax better, poop better, or work out better.
  • Supplements may be ubiquitous, but many experts have serious reservations about their rise.
  • Still, there are exceptions to every rule—and supplements are no different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These days, it seems like everyone is taking a supplement—to look better, think better, sleep better, relax better, poop better, or work out better. And you’re not imagining things: Half of adults and one-third of children in the United States take supplements regularly, according to the Office of Dietary Supplements.

Supplements may be ubiquitous, but many experts have serious reservations about their rise. First, most physicians recommend obtaining nutrients directly from food rather than a pill or capsule. Second, supplements aren’t reviewed for safety and effectiveness by the FDA before they hit shelves. Because of all the concerns surrounding supplements, Jeffrey Linder, MD, MPH, a general internist and professor of medicine at the Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, takes a dim view of the category overall: In fact, “a vast majority of supplements are probably worthless,” he tells SELF.

Still, there are exceptions to every rule—and supplements are no different. Many experts, as it turns out, do take some type of supplement, but they are choosy about which ones they select. Read on to learn more about six they actually use.

Recent findings suggest that how it works: Vitamin D plays key roles in bone health and immune function. In fact, low vitamin D is associated with a wide swath of medical conditions, according to Dr. Linder—including cancer, autoimmune diseases, infectious diseases, and cardiovascular complications (and, famously, seasonal affective disorder, or SAD).

Why some docs like it: Vitamin D deficiency is widespread, especially among people who live at northern latitudes that don’t see as much sun during the winter, and people with darker skin. What’s more, few foods contain significant amounts of vitamin D, so it’s tough to source enough from your diet. Lawrence Green, MD, a dermatologist and clinical professor at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences, tells SELF that these two factors make vitamin D a rare nutrient “we do need to take supplements for.” Nearly every single one of the eight doctors who spoke with SELF for this article said they take a vitamin D supplement, especially in the winter, though the frequency and dosage varied.

In a recent development, what to keep in mind: Most docs recommend vitamin D3 (also known as cholecalciferol) over vitamin D2 (also known as ergocalciferol), as studies have shown that D3 is more effective at raising vitamin D levels in your blood. Whichever option you decide on, try to take it with food—specifically, an item that contains fat. Because vitamin D is a fat-soluble nutrient, it “absorbs better that way,” Sara Velayati, MD, an obesity medicine specialist at Montefiore Einstein and an assistant professor at Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York City, tells SELF. For this reason, Dr. Green makes a point of taking his supplements with breakfast or dinner. “The fattier and thicker the meal,” the better, he states.

Sources indicate that what it does: Calcium is a mineral that helps build and maintain strong bones and teeth. Women in their 40s approaching menopausal age should make it a particular priority to ensure their intake is adequate, Rachel Pessah-Pollack, MD, an endocrinologist at NYU Langone Health and a clinical professor at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine, tells SELF, as the physical changes that come with perimenopause and menopause can heighten bone loss and downstream health conditions like osteoporosis.

Sources indicate that who takes it: Like the other supplements on this list, calcium is best sourced from your diet, Dr. Pessah-Pollack states. “But if you’re not able to (I try to get dairy products but often come up short), a supplement is needed.” She takes a combined calcium and vitamin D tablet daily, as vitamin D helps calcium absorb.

How to take it: “The type of calcium supplements you are taking matters,” Dr. Pessah-Pollack claims. Calcium carbonate and calcium citrate are the two most common. “Calcium carbonate should be taken with food because it requires gastric acid to be absorbed,” Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. Calcium citrate is an alternative that can be taken with or without food.

Sources indicate that how it works: Magnesium is a mineral that can enhance sleep and muscle recovery. Research has also shown that it’s effective at preventing migraines, Raquel Zemtsov, MD, MPH, a family medicine doctor and assistant professor at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, tells SELF.

Why some docs like it: In addition to Dr. Zemtsov, who takes magnesium to stave off migraine symptoms, Dr. Velayati takes magnesium for the sleep benefits. Likewise, Sheeva Talebian, MD, a reproductive endocrinologist at CCRM Fertility of New York, and Kathleen Jordan, MD, an internal medicine physician and chief medical officer at Midi Health, also turn to it at bedtime to boost their shut-eye.

In a recent development, what to keep in mind: Some types of magnesium are better tolerated, claims Dr. Velayati—something to note if you’re especially sensitive to side effects. Magnesium glycinate “avoids the gastrointestinal upset caused by magnesium oxides and magnesium citrates,” for example, Dr. Jordan says. Depending on your needs, however, magnesium glycinate might not be the best option: Magnesium oxide is the recommended magnesium type for migraines, so that’s the one Dr. Zemtsov keeps on hand, for example. Taking magnesium with food can also help prevent GI distress, according to Dr. Velayati.

Sources indicate that how it works: Omega-3 fatty acids are polyunsaturated fats that are key for cardiovascular health. Common omega-3 supplements include fish oil and krill oil.

In a recent development, why some docs like it: Dr. Jordan, Dr. Talebian, and Dr. Velayati all take omega-3s. “With their anti-inflammatory properties and association with improved brain health, this is a popular supplement among physicians, myself included,” Dr. Jordan, who takes krill oil, indicates. Similarly, Dr. Velayati dabbles in fish oil, but takes it selectively. “The right dose really depends on the goal, but I don’t think it’s necessary for everyone,” she says.

What to keep in mind: Fish oil supplements can have a characteristic fishy aftertaste, so it might take some trial and error to find one that works for you (read: doesn’t leave you gagging). What’s more, absorption and bioavailability can be a challenge, according to Dr. Jordan. Because omega-3s, like vitamin D, are fat-soluble, taking fish oil with a meal that contains fat can help skirt this problem. Some claim krill oil doesn’t cause the dreaded aftertaste as much as fish oil, and evidence suggests it’s also better absorbed by the body.

Recent findings suggest that how it works: Iron, a mineral, acts as an essential ingredient in hemoglobin, a protein found in your red blood cells. Without enough iron, your blood won’t be able to carry out its core task of delivering oxygen to organs and tissues, resulting in anemia.

Sources indicate that why some docs like it: Iron deficiency is common in women due to the loss of blood during menstruation every month. “Occasionally, despite trying my hardest to seek out iron-rich foods, I still develop an iron deficiency,” Dr. Zemtsov says. When that happens, she takes ferrous gluconate (a particular type of iron supplement) every other day to treat or prevent anemia, since research demonstrates iron supplements are better absorbed and cause fewer side effects that way. Dr. Jordan also takes iron supplements, citing the advantages for sleep, hair health, and overall energy.

What to keep in mind: Iron absorption is enhanced by vitamin C, so pairing your iron supplement with a food that contains vitamin C or even a vitamin C supplement—as Dr. Zemtsov does—can be helpful.

How it works: Fiber, a type of carb, boosts digestion in a variety of ways: It keeps you full, helps prevent constipation, and supports bowel health. Besides the GI stuff, it also serves other functions in your body, including stabilizing your blood sugar and lowering “bad” LDL cholesterol.

In a recent development, why some docs like it: “Unless you are that rare woman who regularly gets in her 25 to 30 grams per day, extra fiber intake is beneficial for almost everyone, and addresses multiple concerns for me personally, including prediabetes and a rising cholesterol level,” Dr. Jordan states. She takes a fiber supplement as needed, on days when she doesn’t manage to hit her goal.

What to keep in mind: If your body isn’t acclimated to a high fiber intake, suddenly bombarding it could cause some digestive distress (think gas and bloating), so start slow to ease the transition. You’ll also need to increase your water intake simultaneously, since fiber requires water to work.

It has been revealed that “When someone is considering a supplement, I usually recommend having a specific reason for taking it”—like a confirmed nutritional deficiency, Dr. Velayati indicates. “Overall, I view supplements as a way to fill a gap, not a substitute for good nutrition, sleep, exercise, and evidence-based medical care.” The bottom line: Supplements are really meant for plugging holes in your diet.

Magnesium is found in fatty fish, leafy greens, whole grains — and the supplement aisle.

The mighty mineral plays many essential roles in our bodies, but can it help tighten the belt buckle?

We checked in with a doctor to find out.

While magnesium can sneakily support weight loss in a few ways, that’s not its main gig.

“Magnesium alone is not a magic bullet for weight loss,” notes Paunel Vukasinov, MD, a dual board-certified internist and obesity medicine specialist with Medical Offices of Manhattan.

“A comprehensive approach including diet, exercise, and other lifestyle changes are essential,” Vukasinov adds.

Here are a few ways magnesium may support weight loss, as explained by Vukasinov.

“Magnesium is not classified as an appetite suppressant,” Vukasinov claims.

Industry observers note that “However, by potentially stabilizing blood sugar and insulin levels, magnesium may reduce cravings and help prevent overeating. This effect can indirectly support weight loss.”.

Vukasinov reminds us that no specific magnesium dosage is prescribed solely for fat loss.

With that in mind, the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for magnesium is:.

Vukasinov indicates that sticking to the RDA ensures you meet your body’s needs without over-supplementing.

“Excessive intake does not enhance weight loss and may lead to adverse effects,” he adds.

According to Vukasinov, it’s best to get magnesium from food since a nutrient-dense diet, including whole foods, boosts your intake of other extra essentials like fiber, which improves overall health.

Here are some foods you can gobble up for the most magnesium:.

If you know your diet isn’t cutting it, you can find magnesium supplements at major retailers, like Wal-Mart and Target, drug stores, or Amazon.

PSA: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) does not check the safety or effectiveness of dietary supplements, so it’s important to choose a reputable brand that undertakes third-party testing to prove the purity and quality of their products.

For some, magnesium supplements may cause a few unsavory side effects, including diarrhea, stomach upset, or cramping.

Sources indicate that remember that there are many forms of magnesium. Vukasinov points out that magnesium citrate or magnesium oxide can have a laxative effect (yikes).

Be sure you’re taking the best dose based on your RDA, and consider taking it with a meal to better avoid side effects.

Magnesium is not a miracle solution for weight loss, but getting enough of it can ensure that your body produces enough energy and gets enough sleep — both play a major hand in weight management.

Taking too much will have you gripping your belly with stomach pain or diarrhea, so stick to the daily recommended amounts.

  • A cross-shaped roof will mark the San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex in Rome, Italy, which Japanese studio Shigeru Ban Architects is designing with local architect Vittorio Petrucci.
  • The church will occupy a presently underused site in Ostia, a coastal neighbourhood for which the project is hoped to become an architectural landmark.
  • The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be constructed with a frame of timber – Ban’s signature material – with a deliberately simple form that is intended to evoke a fabric tent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Shigeru Ban Architects.

A cross-shaped roof will mark the San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex in Rome, Italy, which Japanese studio Shigeru Ban Architects is designing with local architect Vittorio Petrucci.

The church will occupy a presently underused site in Ostia, a coastal neighbourhood for which the project is hoped to become an architectural landmark.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be constructed with a frame of timber – Ban’s signature material – with a deliberately simple form that is intended to evoke a fabric tent.

According to Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci, the overarching goal is for the church to help establish a greater sense of community and place in the area, which they describe as having a “fragmented urban fabric”.

“We wanted to design a place of worship that also brings the whole community together,” stated Ban.

Sources indicate that “The timber structure expresses the idea of a tent, a simple, welcoming form that connects people with one another and with their surroundings. Through this project, we hope architecture can help create a upcoming sense of belonging in the neighbourhood.”.

Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci’s proposal was the winning entry of a competition for the church.

It is one of five winning designs selected as part of the Fresh Churches Programme – an initiative led by the local church district, the Diocese of Rome, and the Italian Episcopal Conference, an assembly of Catholic bishops, to provide permanent homes for parish communities in the region.

As part of the project, four new churches will be built, while one existing parish complex will be extended.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be built on a raised public plaza, with various parish facilities, community spaces and a priest’s residence embedded below.

In a recent development, its key feature will be its angular roof, which is shaped like a cross but not immediately readable as one. This is modelled on a latent cross – a feature in sacred architecture, in which a cross shape is integrated in the spatial design, without being clearly visible.

Inside, the church will have a diamond-shaped proposal, with large stained-glass windows positioned in the four cardinal directions. They will be triangular in shape and feature designs modelled on neighbourhood street art.

The project will be complete with a landscaped park, as well as various recreational and sports facilities, which the studios noted will “create opportunities for social interaction and everyday activities”.

Industry observers note that the San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex is not the first church project by Ban. Among his others is the landmark Cardboard Cathedral in Newly introduced Zealand, which is formed of 98 cardboard tubes combined with wood and polycarbonate. We named it the most significant building of 2013 in our list of the 25 most significant buildings of the 21st century.

Other Italian church proposals recently featured on Dezeen include Stefano Boeri Architetti’s design for the Ambrosian Monastery in Milan, which will have a sail-like roof form.

Images courtesy of Shigeru Ban Architects.
